subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR COOPERATION IN MATTERS OF HEALTH AND HEALTH INSURANCE

speechtext:
Hon. H. A. BRUCE (Parkdale) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 7, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.
He said: This is a reintroduction of a bill which was not reached last session. The purpose of this bill is to provide that the Unemployment Insurance Commission created* by the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, shall cooperate with other authorities in the dominion or provinces for the purpose of collecting information concerning any plan for providing medical care or compensation in cases of ill health.
These provisions were found in the Employment and Social Insurance Act, chapter 38 of the statutes of 1935. This act, having been declared to be ultra vires by majority of the supreme court, and subsequently by a judgment of the privy council delivered January 28, 1937, was repealed in 1940 by section 103 of chapter 44 of the statutes of that year, being the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.
The competency of parliament to legislate in regard to unemployment insurance has been now settled by the amendment to the British North America Act of 1940. It is highly desirable to reintroduce these health provisions into our dominion law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I answer this question orally? With reference to question 1, "Has the attention of the government been drawn to Mr. H. G. Wells' statement", I should like to say that much depends upon what my hon. friend means by the attention of the government being drawn to a matter. His question, of course, draws the attention of the government to the matter, otherwise I am not aware that the attention of the government has been drawn to the point which he has raised. In that connection I would like to point out that it is very difficult to answer questions of the kind because, without conferring with all departments of the government to ascertain whether any communications of the character mentioned have been received, it would not be possible to give a definite reply of yes or no. I would like to suggest with reference to questions where a particular point of information is sought that the specific matter on which information is desired be set forth. The indefinite form, "has the attention of the government been drawn to certain communications" invariably creates some difficulty in the preparation of a reply.
Answering question 2, Mr. Strasser is not receiving any arms and he is not raising any armed forces, so there is no action which the government could take or will take in the matter. While I am speaking of this question I should also like to refer to question 36.

*

2.	Is the government aware that Otto Strasser applied for a visa to reenter the United States and that his application has been refused?
3.	Is it true that Otto Strasser is raising an armed force in Canada in connection with his leadership of a so-called free Germany?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Part 3 of question 36 is practically the same question that I have just answered, "Is it true that Otto Strasser is raising an armed force in Canada in connection with his leadership of a so-called free Germany?" If I might be permitted to answer that question now, I would say that it is not true.
Answering questions 1 and 2 I would say that there were certain reasons of public policy which governed the matter of Mr. Strasser's admission to Canada, and if the hon. member who has asked the question would seek an interview with the Undersecretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Robertson will be pleased to let him see the confidential correspondence on the matter.

This raises a question
which I have had up with my hon. friend; that is to say, whether we should disclose the number of men serving. I have tried to meet the convenience of, and -provide information for, hon. members as far as possible, by giving round figures-that is to say, upwards of so many, rather than giving actual figures. I trust the -house will accept that as being sufficient in connection with matters of this kind.

Well,
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the minister takes that attitude at this time, but I would suggest to him that this is a substantial change of policy, and possibly of very recent date. On November 12, 1941, as reported in Hansard, page 4322, in answer to a question relating t-o the total number of men now serving in overseas theatres of war, the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), then acting as Associate Minister of National Defence, gave the exact figure,

Motions for Papers
indicating that, as of October 25, 1941, 110,209 were serving in all theatres beyond Canada. As a matter of fact, the minister himself, in the course of a speech on November 5, and in reply to a question from my colleague the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mr. Casselman) stated that there were over 110,000 serving.
If the minister mentions that these figures can only be given in round numbers, I should like to point out to him that his margin of inaccuracy was only 209.
Similarly, at page 4323 of Hansard, November 12,	1941, the Associate Minister of
National Defence gave the exact figures of the total number of men then serving in all branches of the Canadian Army.
It is apparent that the objection which is now taken to furnishing statistics of strength represents a very recent change of policy, and I do say that the minister should give us a reason for that change. I should like to make it clear that I am not at the moment quarrelling with the policy; I want to know what it is, and the reasons therefor.
While I am about it I might also refer to Nos. 8 and 9 under Motions for Papers on the order paper. No. 8 deals with the air force, and No. 9 with the navy. I might say that I helped draft these motions, and in these cases inquiry, has not been made regarding the number serving overseas, because I understood it was the policy of both the naval and the air force departments which they have consistently taken and maintained, that these figures should not be furnished. Now there is a change of policy on the part of the Department of National Defence regarding the army. I should like to know the reasons for that change so that they may be considered, having regard to the fact that heretofore we have been given exact figures.

My hon. friend knows
that in only the one case to. which he has referred were the actual figures given.
Yes.

I may say to my hon. friend that that was a slip. That should not have been done. The house will realize, I am sure, that you can no more get those figures in England than you can fly to the moon. They won't give them at all. Unfortunately we adopted in the one instance the policy-which I think was wrong-of giving figures. I am willing, although here I may be going too far, to give figures of enlistments even. I only want hon. members to realize that in withholding figures we are acting simply in the interests of security. I do not see why we should publish on the
pages of Hansard the exact size of our army, our navy or our air force. It is all very well for the enemy to guess about it, but there is no reason in the world why responsible ministers should stand up in their places and give that information. I do not believe that precise figures were ever given before. The hon. gentleman cited the case in which I spoke of "over 110,000". If it had not been that the previous figures were given there might have been a wide margin and that would have been the minimum, whereas, if you give the exact figures it discloses of course the maximum as well.
It might not be objectionable to give hon. members individually the exact figures, although there, perhaps, I may be going farther than I should. Let me say that I would have no objection to giving exact figures to some hon. member who wishes to check them to make sure he is not being misled, and I do propose to give the house "upwards of so-and-so", or, as I said in that case, "over so-and-so".
I hope the house will accept that suggestion as being, to say the least, not too restricted, and going perhaps further than ministers would go elsewhere.

I have no desire to pursue the matter: I have asked the minister for his reasons, and he has now given them. I may point out, however, that in the United States the policy to which he takes exception is being followed; the nation is being told from time to time what the strength of the army is.
No.

speechtext:
["On Thursday last the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) asked what effect the order in council advancing time one hour would have upon the Atlantic standard time zone. He pointed out that in that portion of Canada within the Atlantic standard time zone already the mean or sun time was in advance' of the actual time and suggested that a great portion of the people of Nova Scotia and all the people of New Brunswick would be ninety-six minutes ahead of true sun time.
Generally speaking, the width of a time zone is 675 miles. The farther westward a point is within this zone the greater the amount by which the mean time varies over the actual time. To illustrate this: Halifax, for example, is 14 minutes ahead of mean time; Moncton, 19 minutes; Saint John, 24 minutes; Fredericton, 27 minutes, and Woodstock, 30 minutes.
This situation, of course, applies not only in the case of Atlantic time but throughout the various time zones in Canada. For example, Ottawa is 3 minutes ahead of sun time; Toronto, 18 minutes; Windsor, 32 minutes, while Fort William is 58 minutes ahead of sun time. Such a situation exists in every time zone, and to attempt to reconcile mean and actual time would, of course, obviously create an impossible situation.
In his question the leader of the opposition correctly stated that other factors, such as transportation, might affect the position. I communicated with the Railway Association of Canada as to the transportation problem which would be involved if any changes were made in the order. On Friday afternoon I received the following reply:
Your message yesterday re adoption daylight saving time in maritimes. Deflection from true sun time at points in maritimes would
not be any more excessive than deflection at many other points throughout Canada. Transportation difficulties resulting from adoption new time in maritimes are not any greater than in any other time zone. Would point out that in 1941 Halifax, Saint John, and Moncton voluntarily adopted daylight saving time from May 4 to September 27. In circumstances we urge that there should be no modification of order in council 547 exempting the ^maritimes as such modification would result in voiding all public time-table and working time-table arrangements already completed on basis of order in council. Also modification would result in disruption of through and local train connections and railway arrangements cannot now be altered."]

speechtext:
On January 28 I was asked a question by the hon. member for Haldimand1 (Mr. Senn), which I agreed to answer at a later time. The question was:
It has been drawn to my attention that there is danger of a serious shortage of cheese boxes, owing to the failure of the controller to release material for manufacture. It has also been drawn to my attention that the same condition exists in regard to milk cans.. It is pointed out that there is an insufficient quantity of tin to coat the cans. Have any representations been made to the minister on this subject, and if so, does he intend to take action?
The answer is that there may be a temporary shortage of cheese boxes at some points during the present winter, owing to the heavy increase in the production of cheese as compared with the same period one year ago. The total gradings of cheese last week exceeded those of the same week one year ago by 889 per cent, while the increase in the accumulative gradings since December 1 last is 207 per cent. Many

of the cheese box manufacturers had not provided for the manufacture of any quantity of boxes during the winter months, and, owing to the increase in the production of cheese, there is a temporary shortage of properly seasoned material for making boxes in some sections. It can be stated, however, that officials of the timber controller's office, also officials of the dairy products division, have investigated the cheese box situation in Ontario and Quebec with reference to a supply of boxes for the coming season, and it is expected that there will be sufficient boxes available to meet the requirements throughout the year.
With regard to milk cans, the tinned iron used in the manufacture of large thirty-gallon milk cans is imported from England, and it is understood that supplies of such material in Canada are satisfactory. The heavy black iron used for making milk and cream cans of five and eight gallons, also for reinforcing the large milk cans, comes from the United States. The General Steel Wares Limited and the Canadian John Wood Company, Toronto, placed orders in the United States for material some time ago, and while only part of their orders has been filled they expect to get priority rating, which will enable them to secure the balance of their orders. The tin situation in Canada is tight; meetings have been held between the agricultural supply board and the officers of the metal controller's office, and action has been taken in an effort to secure the necessary tin to meet the requirements of the daily industry.

On January 29 the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) asked me a question, as follows:
I should like to draw attention to order in council P.C. 8126, dated October 22, 1941, but published only on January 23, 1942, in an extra

Prairie Farm Income Payments
edition of the Canada Gazette. My first question to the Minister of Agriculture is, why was the publication of this order in council so long delayed? What other steps were taken to bring its provisions to the attention of the interested public?
The answer to that question is that the War Measures Act does not require the publication of orders, in council passed under the act. The practice in this department has been to publish such orders in council when it is desired to bring, through the Canada Gazette, the information contained in the order to those to whom it is intended to apply. In the case of this order more direct communication was the means of conveyance. This took the form of press and radio announcements and press advertisements. Following this publicity a number of applications were received for copies of the order and, since it was apparent that a considerable number would likely be required for distribution through this department and the treasury department, it was decided to have the order printed in the Gazette and the necessary copies obtained for distribution.
The next question was:
The order in council provides for the expenditure of $20,000,000 by way of additional payments to increase the income of farmers in the spring wheat area of western Canada. I should like the minister to explain the real purpose of this order in council, and the relationship of the payments to be made under it to the $35,000,000 provided under schedule B of Appropriation Act No. 4 of 1941.
The answer is that the amount of money, $20,000,000, provided in the order in council, was for the purpose of supplying additional income to wheat farmers who had harvested a much lighter crop during the past year than was expected at the time the policy was laid down last spring. There is no direct relationship between the $20,000,000 and the $35,000-
000.	The $35,000,000 provided under order in council last year was for the purpose of encouraging a reduction in wheat acreage. That reduction was made, and there was also a reduction in the crop because of the unusual weather conditions this summer, which cut down the revenue from wheat sufficiently, as we thought, to warrant the government in voting an additional $20,000,000 for that purpose.
The last question was:
May I also ask him to tell this house why those provisions were made by order in council instead of being brought before parliament at its November sitting in the usual and proper manner.
As is indicated, the order was issued on October 22. The regulations under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act require that all applications for payments be in before December 1;
and in order to get information out to the farmers in sufficient time to allow those applications to be in by December 1 it was considered necessary to take this action immediately rather than wait for a sitting of the house.

Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): On Friday the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), as reported in Hansard, page 193, addressed a question to me orally in the following words:
I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services to an editorial appearing on page 4 of Boating Magazine for January-February of this year, under the caption " Fairmile Fuddle." I shall not read the editorial, because I presume
'Fairmile Fuddle'

the minister has a copy of the journal. I should like to ask these questions: First, where are the five boats which are reported to have left Midland early in November, 1941, and, second, was a qualified officer in charge of those boats?
I stated to my hon. friend when he asked the question that he had not given notice of it. I find now that he had written to me. His letter reached my office about one o'clock on Friday, but at that time I was in attendance at a meeting of the cabinet council and did not return again to my office before coming into the house at three o'clock. So that I did not have my hon. friend's letter when I answered his question. I have it now, and having looked into the matter, I should like to make the following statement.
In late November, arrangements were made for two Fairmile motor launches from Midland and two from Penetanguishene to sail in company to Toronto, a distance of approximately 600 miles. One great lakes pilot was employed for the Midland group and another for the Penetanguishene group. All four motor launches had commanding officers who were lieutenants, Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, who had experience ranging from two years' war service in a Canadian destroyer to one year's service in motor torpedo boats, as well as peace time experience in handling small craft. In addition, a senior officer was appointed in this group of four Fairmiles for the passage. This officer, Lieutenant-Commander McQueen, R.C.N.V.R., has a master's' great lakes ticket and was a great lakes pilot for vessels in his own company during peace time. In addition this officer served during the last war as an officer in tjie Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, originally in submarine chasers and later in the salvage branch of the Admiralty. Therefore, it can be taken that this officer was not merely competent, but wTas an officer of very great experience.
The two Fairmile motor launches from Midland, Q-058 and Q-051, sailed at eight a.m. on November 24. Q-058 had on board a great lakes pilot and Q-051 was instructed to follow close astern. Unfortunately a very heavy blizzard set in almost immediately. Q-051 lost sight of Q-058, got into shoal water and struck one propeller on a rock. There was no damage to her hull and she eventually proceeded in company with the other three vessels. This Fairmile was eventually hauled up for repairs at Sarnia, which is roughly half way between the point of departure and Toronto, where it was found that a new shaft and propeller would be required. The total 
cost will not exceed Si,200. The remaining three Fairmiles proceeded to Toronto where they arrived safely on November 30.
On this date the weather conditions in the lower St. Lawrence were so severe that it was considered that no further Fairmile launches could be sailed to Halifax this season owing to the probability of damage from ice. Instructions, therefore, were given for these three to be laid up at Toronto for the winter and the fourth at Sarnia. Slight damage to Q-072, not exceeding 8270, occurred while she was being hauled out at Toronto. The total repairs wall cost less than $1,500, it is estimated, to ships that are worth $600,000, or a repair cost of about one quarter of one per cent. These repairs are not properly classed as "extensive and costly", the words used in this editorial.
The Fairmile motor launches are of wooden construction and could not be employed where they would encounter ice. All thirty-six Fairmiles will be in commission by early summer. They will he extremely usefully employed in anti-submarine patrols off the coast of Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Labrador, and in the gulf of St. Lawrence. It would not be -possible to spare any for use in the Mediterranean.

The hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) asked a question on Friday about a report that 100 commodities are not affected by the price ceiling. This report was incorrect. Seasonal goods are definitely under the price ceiling, as the board and its administrators have repeatedly stated, and there is nothing that this board has said or done to warrant any misunderstanding in this connection. The report has no foundation whatever.
Seasonal spring and summer goods, not similar to goods sold during the basic period, September 15 to October 11, 1941, are subject to the general rule that they may not be priced higher than they would have been priced if they had been sold in the basie period. This means that in the spring of 1942 seasonal goods may not be sold at more than the price charged in the spring of 1941, plus an increase equivalent to the increase between the spring of 1941 and the autumn of 1941, in the price of year-round goods of the nearest similar classification and intrinsic value.

Munitions and Supply-Contractors
For the practical application, of this general principle, the board has issued a list of seasonal goods, has advised manufacturers that their 1942 prices must be approved by the administrator of their industry in consultation with the administrator of retail trade, and has advised wholesalers and retailers that they may buy at approved manufacturers' prices and add the same mark-up as they did during the corresponding season in 1941.

speechtext:
On Thursday last the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) asked what effect the order in council advancing time one hour would have upon the Atlantic standard time zone. He pointed out that in that portion of Canada within the Atlantic standard time zone already the mean or sun time was in advance' of the actual time and suggested that a great portion of the people of Nova Scotia and all the people of New Brunswick would be ninety-six minutes ahead of true sun time.
Generally speaking, the width of a time zone is 675 miles. The farther westward a point is within this zone the greater the amount by which the mean time varies over the actual time. To illustrate this: Halifax, for example, is 14 minutes ahead of mean time; Moncton, 19 minutes; Saint John, 24 minutes; Fredericton, 27 minutes, and Woodstock, 30 minutes.
This situation, of course, applies not only in the case of Atlantic time but throughout the various time zones in Canada. For example, Ottawa is 3 minutes ahead of sun time; Toronto, 18 minutes; Windsor, 32 minutes, while Fort William is 58 minutes ahead of sun time. Such a situation exists in every time zone, and to attempt to reconcile mean and actual time would, of course, obviously create an impossible situation.
In his question the leader of the opposition correctly stated that other factors, such as transportation, might affect the position. I communicated with the Railway Association of Canada as to the transportation problem which would be involved if any changes were made in the order. On Friday afternoon I received the following reply:
Your message yesterday re adoption daylight saving time in maritimes. Deflection from true sun time at points in maritimes would
not be any more excessive than deflection at many other points throughout Canada. Transportation difficulties resulting from adoption new time in maritimes are not any greater than in any other time zone. Would point out that in 1941 Halifax, Saint John, and Moncton voluntarily adopted daylight saving time from May 4 to September 27. In circumstances we urge that there should be no modification of order in council 547 exempting the ^maritimes as such modification would result in voiding all public time-table and working time-table arrangements already completed on basis of order in council. Also modification would result in disruption of through and local train connections and railway arrangements cannot now be altered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that my hon. friend the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) is to be the first speaker in this debate this afternoon. He is, as I think hon. members are well aware, a close personal friend of my own and I had hoped to be in the house while he was speaking, but I may say to him that I have not yet had an opportunity to-day of so much as looking at the mail that has come in over the week-end. The morning has been taken up with other matters, among them the representations of important delegations which occupied my

time exclusively from 10.30 this morning until after two o'clock this afternoon. I have been in the house from three until now twenty past four. I am trying to give all the time I possibly can to the very important matters immediately connected with the war effort of the country. That involves of necessity my absence from the house a good part of the time during the course of the debate. I know my hon. friend will excuse me if I am not present when he is speaking. I raise the matter because I noticed that by some of tiie press attention had been drawn to the fact that one day of last week when the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) was speaking I found it necessary because of an engagement at the time, made before I knew at all that the hon. member was to speak, to leave the house and keep that engagement along with others [DOT]which I had for the afternoon. I hope the house will realize that I am anxious to be as courteous as I can be to every hon. member, but it will be recognized that in addition to all the matters in connection with the war effort to which the government is obliged to give attention there is a good deal in the way of political controversy both in and out of parliament. I hope it will not be thought that any actions of mine are intended to be a reflection in any way upon those who may be taking part in political discussions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must first thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for his very kind reference to myself and assure him that I know he has a tremendous load to carry and cannot be in the house at all times. I must also thank the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) for his kindly remarks.
FEBRUARY 2, 1942	[DOT]
The Address-Mr. MacNicol
There has been enough said during this debate to convince me that many of the members of this house and many outside this house apparently are not yet seized of the stern and grim realities of this war and of the fact that this empire of which Canada, in my opinion and that of many others, is an indissoluble part, irrespective of the statute of Westminster and any other statute, is engaged in a life and death struggle which can have only one ending, either victory, freedom and life, or defeat, bondage and death.
We are receiving from all across this empire reports from the generals commanding our armies on the far-flung battle-line that more fighting battalions and more munitions are required if the empire is to be saved. I have heard here, from men in high places, that fighting battalions are not now and have not been the matter of major importance. I will ask each hon. member to cast his thoughts across the seas. Last year our armies retired from Libya. Now they have again retreated. Why? Our armies evacuated Greece and Crete. Why? Our men were captured at Kowloon and Hong Kong. Why? Our troops have now retired from Malaya. Why? To me the answer is very clear: our armies have not had, and have not now, sufficient fighting troops and munitions.
The speech from the throne, as I read it and understand what is behind it, lays bare the stern fact that more fighting battalions and munitions are required. But it does not say that these battalions and munitions will be rapidly provided. It proposes that there shall be a delay, at least as regards the provision of the battalions, until a plebiscite is taken-a matter of perhaps three months-a plebiscite which will be both costly to the country and heart-rending to the people.
My honoured leader in a brilliant speech pointed a way to relieve the situation I have mentioned, which, at least to me, is clearly indicated in the speech from the throne. He advocated an amendment to the speech from the throne in which he called for a prompt mobilization of all our material resources and, on a selective basis, the full man and woman power of the nation. I am not in favour of a plebiscite but am in favour of the amendment. According to the press-which may not have the facts-a plebiscite will cost this country anything between $800,000 and $3,000,000, altogether too large a sum to spend when the government itself is asking the people of this country to economize in every way they can, and has even ordered the cutting down of sugar rations; when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is going out for one of the largest loans in the history of this country
-a loan which must be subscribed; nothing should interfere with that-and when nearly everybody in this country will shortly have to pay the most staggering income tax which they have ever had to meet, and that a month earlier than on any previous occasion. In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, this is not a time to spend up to $3,000,000 in taking a plebiscite.
When I was home a few days ago I was greatly alarmed as to what might be the effect of the decision to take a plebiscite on the minister obtaining, from several sources, contributions to the war loan. A number of parents told me that their children, school children, had said that if the government is going to squander $3,000,000 or so in taking a plebiscite, they will refuse to buy any more war savings stamps. I hope it does not have that effect on the school children of Canada, because one of the things on which I can congratulate the government is their having persuaded children to buy war savings stamps. It has three good effects. It teaches school children thrift at an impressionable age; it inculcates patriotism, which they learn in contributing their pennies for stamps; and it turns a lot of money into the treasury of this country. Returns from the Toronto public and secondary schools show that subscriptions by children between September, 1940, and December, 1941, both inclusive, amounted to $434,641.08. That is in addition to contributions by them of almost $50,000 to some thirty-eight other war service organizations, of which amount $16,929.25 was given to the Toronto Telegram war victims fund, and $13,271.43 to the Red Cross fund. I hope the controversy caused by the taking of a plebiscite will not affect children's donations, because, if it does, I would fear it would affect the purchases of war savings certificates by their parents- purchases which have had a good effect on the average humble parent, teaching him to save his money against the rainy day which may come. I hope that the government will not proceed with the taking of a plebiscite, but will find some other way to accomplish what is required to be done.
We are told that the government will have to break a promise. Well, a bad promise is always better broken than kept; and it was, in my humble opinion, a bad promise. It is bad because it was made, years ago, to retain political strength in this country; it is bad because it should not have been made, particularly in war. time, for none can tell how war will go. Generals who expect to win for their side endeavour to place the most men and the most machinery at the point of fighting, first; but we are now undertaking to enrol an army for the purpose of taking a

The Address-Mr. MacNicol
plebiscite across the country, while we should be enrolling men and providing fighting battalions, to be sent wherever the fight is taking place.
A bad promise, as I have said, is much better broken than kept. It is humiliating for a government that has the great following behind it that this government has, the largest in the history of the country, to be placed in the position, through a political promise made in war time, of being compelled for a time to cease its work in the raising of battalions and the making of munitions in order to take a plebiscite. It makes me think of the giant of antiquity, made of metal but with feet of clay. Here we have a government, the strongest government the country ever had, throttled by a promise. Its feet are so tangled up by its promise not to enrol men for overseas, either on a selective or on a compulsory *basis, that it can do nothing in that regard.
Let me discuss for a few minutes something else in connection with the government's prosecution of the war. I refer to the high cost of recruiting under the present system, which would all be saved under a system such as that in force in the United States. I was in western Ontario recently and spent a couple of days in a small village. There I saw on the lawn of the town hall a tent and a couple of recruiting officers-there may have been more. There were two during the day, but w'hether that was the total number I do not know. I engaged them in conversation. I asked them how many recruits were coming forward, and they told me that they had been there ten days and had obtained two recruits. What a big price to pay to obtain' two recruits! They told me that in a town ten miles west of that point there was also a tent on the lawn of the town hall with two officers in charge of recruiting, and that in the space of two weeks they had obtained only one recruit.
I have seen a similar situation in many towns across Canada, and I have no doubt it is true of the country as a whole. We are paying a staggering price to obtain small results. I saw a long cavalcade of trucks-I do not remember exactly how many-going up Yonge street, Toronto, on one occasion, and I inquired w'here they were going. I was informed that they were on their way to northern Ontario to carry on a recruiting campaign. Well, that was a large number of men and trucks to send to northern Ontario for that purpose. It would be rather expensive, for there were billboards here and there as well as advertisements, and there would be the cost of the trucks, the gasoline and so forth.

-which will be required to take the plebiscite. A few days ago I saw in the Toronto Globe and Mail a picture of the Ridley family in the city of Brantford-one of our best industrial cities. This picture showed two sons and two daughters, all four of whom have enlisted and one of whom is in the army in Great Britain. I was surprised that the hon. member for Brantford City, having seen what he saw in Great Britain, could come back and take the stand he did, not to send without a plebiscite immediate help to Lieutenant Kenneth Ridley, his townsman, whom he perhaps saw or who, in any event, is in England. I was surprised and sorry, because I have a very warm feeling for the hon. member for Brantford City.
The Address-Mr. MacNicol

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) recently made a statement that I endorse. I cannot say very much about the Minister of Agriculture at any time, because I know little about agriculture. I am not like some hon. members who know a great deal about agriculture and at the same time know all about what it took me thirty years to learn, the manufacture of iron and steel.

speechtext: You are not a lawyer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I was not referring to lawyers; I was referring mostly to certain hon. gentlemen to my left.
The Minister of Agriculture, in a speech delivered, I believe, on January 10, stated that this government would not fail to send strong support-let me quote his words:
We are also going to take our part in manning the bastions of empire in any part of the world.
I was pleased to read that, and I hope the minister will speed up the sending of support to these bastions of empire, not delay it as in the sending of it to the great bastion of Hong Kong.	.
Last summer I was in Saskatchewan, and on the day I was in Regina, September 11, I was affected by reading a page in the Regina Leader-Post giving the pictures and names of heroes of that province, of whom twelve were killed in the navy, sixteen in the army and forty-nine in the air force. We have always thrilled with pride at what our army has done, and I have on more than one occasion read of some famous fighter from Saskatchewan, whose name has slipped my mind for a moment, but across the skies over France and Germany these Saskatchewan fighters have blazed a bright trail of glory that will never fade. I could say the same about my own province and every province, but as I come from Ontario perhaps it is not out of place for me to say a word about my own province, because we hear so many unkind things said about it in this house-it rolls off my back like water from a duck's back; the most sticks are always under the best apple tree, and I take it in that way. My own city of Toronto with its suburbs has sent more men to the army in this war, as it did in the last war, than any other equal community in this country. My own riding sent more men overseas in the last war than any other riding bar none, and to-day the sons of the heroes of 1914-1918 of Davenport riding have enlisted in their thousands to fight anywhere in the world. Most of their parents, I might say, are old country stock.
Something has been said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and I was sorry he said what he did, because I have a
	.
very warm feeling for him, for reasons about which I do not care to speak. But the other day he said something about the so-called committee of Two Hundred. And they have been spoken of contemptuously by an hon. gentleman on my right who did not know anything whatever about them, and by an hon. gentleman to your right, Mr. Speaker, who perhaps knew less. That committee consists of two hundred or more outstanding men and women. They come, not from Toronto alone but from most of the towns and cities of Ontario and perhaps every county of lower Ontario at least, if not every county in Ontario. They did not sign as Conservatives or Liberals. I have not looked to see what they are politically; many of them I know, and I give them credit for being sincere. We are all entitled to be regarded as sincere. Many of them have sons overseas. I do not blame them a bit for doing what they can to shake the government out of its complacency; someone has to do it, and I am sure that if the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) could only have his fling, he could do a much bigger job than he is doing to-day. It is no fault of his; I will add that.
I see my time is going. I should like to talk a little now about munitions, because iron and steel have been woven into my very fabric from boyhood. A couple of years ago I offered in this house the suggestion that this government at once initiate measures to increase the production of iron in this country. At that time I said the day would come when Canada might not have the iron it needed to make munitions. I hope that time is not approaching, but the situation looks very serious. For some time we have had a delegation at Washington coaxing the steel controller there to permit us to get some iron and steel, and at last he has consented to give us two million tons of iron and steel. That is not very much for the programme outlined by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe); but what about next year?
I beg this government to delay no longer but immediately to promote the production of pig-iron. My suggestion two years ago was that this government grant a bonus to encourage that production, but I was turned down; my words fell on deaf ears. But thanks to Premier Hepburn, who has been denounced here so frequently, some action was taken. He carried out the programme first initiated by the Ferguson government, and granted a bonus of $2 a ton on the production of pig-iron. I am happy to say that in the county in which I lived when I was a young man, the county of Algoma-it was the district of Algoma then-the Algoma steel company at

The Address-Mr. MacNicol
Sault Ste Marie is now producing considerable quantities of pig-iron from a low grade ore possessing, I believe, less than fifty per cent iron content, and requiring to be beneficiated.
I have not been able to obtain the latest figures, but I believe the annual production is something like four or five hundred thousand tons. That is a substantial production. I ask the government now to do what it can, by means of a bonus to the Algoma steel company or any other company, to double the production of pig-iron, because next year we may not be able to obtain any from the United States, whose reserves are being rapidly depleted. I made a careful study of this matter some years ago, and according to the best figures the reserves in sight in the United States amount to about five billion tons. This year they are producing some eighty-five million tons, while the production next year probably will be double that if they carry out their vast programme. We may not be able to get any iron from the United States if this war continues and they go at it as they are planning to do.
We have plenty of iron ore in Canada. We have a high grade of hematite at Steep Rock. I do not know what is being done about that, or how soon we may take advantage of it; but the government should see to it that Steep Rock comes into operation just as soon as possible, because that is a really high grade ore. Then we have billions of tons of low grade ore as well. In the United States they are now looking for low grade iron ore, because the Ford company has developed an electrolytic process by means of which iron can be economically produced from ore with a content of from twenty to thirty per cent, which heretofore has been considered of no account. In the Hudson bay basin we have billions of tons of low grade ore; and if they can use it in the United States, we can use it here. So I urge the government to take steps to bring about a much greater production of iron in this country.
There is one other item about which I should like to say a word, namely, magnesium metal. I raised that question on June 14 last. At that time the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) did not seem to know much about it; he said some company was going to build a plant on the Gatineau river, but that plant was for making magnesium oxide, not for magnesium metal. The United States is going into this in a big way, and Germany has been producing large quantities of this metal. It may be that their planes have been able to do the things they have because they have so much magnesium metal in their construction. It weighs one-third less
than aluminum and has approximately the same tensile strength. A plane made of magnesium metal will go faster and carry a larger load of bombs further. I urge this government to get into the business. We have one of the greatest deposits in the world of dolomite limestone, from which magnesium metal is made, together with any amount of electrical horse-power, which is essential in the manufacturing process.
I want now to say a word about Canadian manufacturers, because they deserve the unstinted .praise of this house and this country for what they have done, commencing even before the war. At their annual spring meeting in 1939, before war broke out, the Canadian Manufacturers association decided to send a committee overseas to consult with the British government and British manufacturers in order to demonstrate what Canadian plants, Canadian workmen, Canadian technicians and engineers could do. And they did go overseas, at their own expense, and, I am glad to say, with the blessing of the government. When they came back, the Prime Minister was very kind; he spoke very nicely of their efforts and gave them due credit. On September 8, in a press release, the Prime Minister said:
With the concurrence of the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom, a delegation organized by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and widely representative of Canadian industry recently visited the United Kingdom to study on the spot all forms of armament and munitions production with a view to the expeditious adaptation of Canadian industry to these forms of production.
They came home and went to work, and they played a major part in organizing this country for the production of munitions. As the Minister of Munitions and Supply has said, Canadian industry did a wonderful job with his help in providing orders, I am happy to say. I have not time to mention the names of all these outstanding men, but I think some of them should appear on our records; I believe they deserve that recognition. Among these business men were: E. Holt Gurney, Toronto; H. G. Bertram, Dundas; E. Winslow-Spragge, Montreal; John E. Goodison, Sarnia; A. R. Goldie, Galt; Victor Drury, Montreal; and Chester Hamilton, Toronto, and John T. Hepburn, Toronto, who were over in Britain, and many others.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe every man or woman in this house is ready to do what he or she can to support the government and the country in order to win this war. It is imperative that we do this. As far as I am concerned, I will go anywhere and do anything the government feel my long experience in industry and manufacturing qualifies
The Address-Mr. MacNicol

me to do in order to assist our war effort. I do not suppose I could go to fight, though if I were placed in a fort, behind a parapet, I might be able to shoot as straight as most people, because in my day I could shoot pretty straight. We have wonderful examples to inspire us. On Sunday, January 25, I went to Grove preparatory school at Lakefield, where a window was unveiled in memory of Sergeant Stuart Dunn, W.A.G., R.C.A.F., a young hero from Quebec city who served over Germany and France for months but who lost his life on a return trip. I liked the spirit of the ceremony. This boy's father, Major C. G. Dunn who had gone to this school also as a lad, and a large number of boys attended the service.. Those young men sang most earnestly the following words, with which I shall conclude:
I vow to thee, my country-all earthly things above-
Entire and whole and perfect, the service of my love.
The love that asks no questions; the love that stands the test,
That lays upon the altar the dearest and the best;
The love that never falters, the love that pays the price,
The love that makes undaunted the final sacrifice.
In memory of what the glorious young heroes from every province of this country have done, it is our duty to send fighting battalions and munitions as speedily as possible to the armies of the empire, no matter where they are.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I must first of all commend the government for the announcement in the speech from the throne regarding the contribution to Great Britain of vast quantities of munitions, foodstuffs and supplies, estimated to be worth at least one billion dollars. May I at the same time commend my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and his advisers for making the financial arrangements necessary for this transaction. I should like to point .out, to him and to them that I am pleased to see that they are at least moving forward and to the left. I trust they are beginning at last to realize how restricted and narrow so-called orthodox finance has been in the past.
I would remind them also of an age-old truth, that so long as the sun shines and the rain falls, so long as we have labour, land and materials in abundance, many things which were deemed impossible a short time ago are now possible. I trust that after this war these will include social justice and social security for all our citizens.

I have listened with a great deal of interest and care to the speeches which have been made so far in this debate, and I have wondered why, in speeches made by the opposition, so little has been said about the great contribution which Canada has made in this war of men, munitions, food, ships and money, as well as other war materials. In the eyes of impartial competent observers, such as the New York Times, this is considered as one of the most astounding accomplishments arising out of this war. This is the way in which they refer to Canada's great contribution of munitions, supplies and other materials.
Prior to coming east for the session, I visited Seattle in connection with a meeting of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission of which I am chairman. I found many of the people in the state of Washington to be loud in their praises of what Canada has done and is doing, but they were extremely critical about their own President Roosevelt. Coming back to Canada, I found numbers of our own people enthusiastic about President Roosevelt, but critical of our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and of Canada's war effort. I am coming to the conclusion that many persons in Great Britain, the United States and Canada are to-day suffering from an affliction which for lack of a better name might be called "far-off pastures look greener affliction," and which, to quite an extent, is affecting their vision of the actual accomplishments of their own country-. I suppose others would diagnose this condition as war nerves.
Speaking about leaders, I am not altogether surprised at the attitude of the Conservative party toward the Prime Minister, the leader of this government, especially when I consider the number of leaders the Conservative party has had during the past number of years and how harshly some of them were treated. Let me take one example only. The best and most capable leader they had in late years, one for whom I have still some admiration, the Right Hon. Viscount Bennett, they forced to leave Canada. No one will deny that the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was and still is a great Canadian. The hearts of that party, however, now incline toward Meighen, but in my estimation Meighen cannot equal Bennett in ability. In passing, may I compliment the present house leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Hanson). Personally I think he has done well as leader. He has certainly worked hard and ably since assuming the responsibility of leader of the opposition; his speech last week was a splendid one, and I wish to compliment him upon it.
In paragraph (c) of his amendment the leader of the opposition regrets that additional

The Address-Mr. Reid
measures for the post-war period were not recommended in the speech from the throne, and before dealing with the question of the plebiscite I should like to remind him that Canada has given more thought and extensive study to post-war conditions and is now further ahead on plans for the post-war period than Great Britain, the United States, or any of the other dominions.
Regarding the matter of holding a plebiscite, may I say at once that I do not like it. When, however, one looks at this matter from a national viewpoint instead of merely a provincial or sectional one, when one faces all the facts he must be convinced that the action proposed by the government, with all the circumstances and facts before them, is the logical one to take. Whether or not we like the plebiscite, its taking has been definitely decided upon by the government, and so the matter should be expedited as speedily as possible. It is unfortunate that at this particular time so much feeling should be aroused or stirred up throughout Canada over the taking of this plebiscite. I do not agree with those who say that the taking of the plebiscite is retarding our war effort.
My personal view on this matter is that there should be complete mobilization of every resource we have in Canada, including finance, natural resources and man-power for service anywhere when considered necessary. So far, the only real sacrifices which have been made by any of our people in this war have been made by those who have given of their lives, who have offered their services to the army, navy or air force, or who are the wives or parents of these boys. Equality of sacrifice is to-day spoken of freely, but we have much further to go in this direction before it becomes an actual reality in Canada. The government have to-day, under the National Resources Mobilization Act, all the powers they require to mobilize finance and industry as well as man-power. I am pleased that the government have intimated to parliament that they are going to do more under these powers than what has been done, splendid as that has been. In my opinion it will require a total all-out war effort to bring victory.
Whilst we are turning out munitions and supplies of all and every kind in commendable quantities and of splendid workmanship, in my opinion we have not yet reached our maximum effort. In certain ways we could do much more than we are doing, and this is especially the situation in British Columbia. In saying this, I have particularly in mind our shipbuilding programme. It is true that we have a programme providing for about $500,000,000 of steel merchant ships, corvettes,
destroyers and other miscellaneous boats, but this is not nearly the total Canadian capacity for producing new ships provided the government, and particularly the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), would only consent to the building of wooden vessels. Will anyone deny that the allies are in need of ships?
It may well be said that the losses at sea so far in this war have not been as heavy as they were during 1914-18, but we should not forget that' our ship tonnage is less to-day than it was during the last war, and we have the further disadvantage of a war in the far east with Japan against us. It is well known that lack of shipping has considerably handicapped Britain's war effort. More and more ships are required to carry vital military supplies and food, not only to Great Britain, Egypt and the near east, but now also to the far east. It is my opinion that Canada's present programme of steel ships cannot now be much further expanded, if at all, owing to the United States war expansion programme recently outlined by President Roosevelt for 1942 and 1943, which programme will require many more million tons of steel than the United States herself required in 1941. Great Britain is crying out for more ships. Great Britain is at the moment short of lumber, to mention but one of her many requirements. Great Britain is at the present time getting lumber from Russia by way of Archangel because she cannot procure all the Canadian lumber on account of lack of ships. Let me read a recent article in the Commercial Intelligence Journal of the Department of Trade and Commerce, of January 17, of this year. The article is headed "Canadian Timber Favoured" and reads:
Examples of the dislike of timber men in Britain to change when once they have become accustomed to certain materials or certain methods of trading are always occurring. When this country began to change from the almost exclusive use of European softwood to the importation of British Columbia pine and hemlock, criticisms about the qualities of this Canadian wood were almost abusive. Many importers stated that they would not have it in their yards; that it was not suitable in building, that it split when nailed, was liable to rot, et cetera. Further, that their workmen disliked it. However, prejudice was gradually overcome, the import grew by leaps and bounds, and owing to circumstances over which the trade has now no control Canadian wood has Since the war constituted our main source of supply. The trade has, in fact, become well accustomed to the wood. Now after a long interval Russian wood is beginning to arrive, but so used to British Columbia pine and hemlock have importers and merchants become that there seems to be no urgent wish to change again. The Russian wood is dearer and this may, of course, have something to do with the
The Address-Mr. Reid

disinclination to purchase when British Columbia pine or hemlock are available. When joinery quality is required, No. 2 common and better British Columbia pine seem to answer all necessary purposes.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that after getting the British .people used to our Canadian lumber and after building up our lumber trade with them, we are at the present time faced with the loss of this trade as a result of the lack of boats. Allow me, sir, to inform the house what we did with regard to ships and wooden shipbuilding during the last war. During those years a total of sixty-nine wooden steamers were built in Canada, twenty-seven of which were built in British Columbia. Every one of these ships carried lumber to Great Britain, taking one and a half million board feet of lumber on each voyage. They were built at a cost of $150,000, compared with five or six hundred thousand dollars, which is the cost of the steel merchant ships being built in Canada at the present time.
When the lion. Minister of Munitions and Supply tells us that wooden ships are too slow, I wonder whether he is overlooking the fact that the ivooden ships built for service during the last war, and which we could build now, made an average speed of 10 or 10J knots an hour. When one considers the average speed of convoys, and the time we had to wait before a ship was available to take military equipment necessary for the Can-dian troops for the defence of Hong Kong, and that when that ship was procured her average speed was only 8J knots an hour, one wonders what really is the chief reason for the opposition to the building of wooden ships. The story of Hong Kong might well have been a different one had we, prior to the fall of Hong Kong had Canadian ships available.
Another instance of where Canada is losing out for lack of ships is in connection with available trade between Canada and South American countries. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) paid, a visit to south America last year with a view to bringing about better trade relations and better relations generally between the peoples of south American countries and Canada, and his mission was, I believe, an unqualified success. He did a great work for Canada on that occasion. However, like many other things we do, we sometimes fail to follow the matter up, and we made a mistake, I believe, in not sending one of our highest officials to represent Canada at the Pan-American conference held a short time ago instead of sending or designating someone to sit in at that conference with what is known to the lawyers as "a watching brief" only. What I want to mention particularly, however, is the fact that although good trade results were obtained

through the visit of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, manufacturers and others in British Columbia cannot carry out the orders which are on their books from south American countries because there are no ships available to transport the goods and articles ordered. In the light of all these facts, I plead with the government, and particularly with the Minister of Munitions and. Supply, as earnestly and sincerely as I can to proceed with the building of wooden ships to augment the programme of steel ships now being built. In British Columbia there are hundreds of idle men ready and competent to work on these ships, both carpenters and caulkers, the two chief types of artisans used, and we have likewise the lumber and other materials in abundance in my province for this class of ship, which is something that cannot truthfully be said with regard to steel.
Since we last met, Canada has declared war on Japan, which now brings the war to Canada's Pacific shore as well as the Atlantic. We in British Columbia are perhaps more directly faced with this menacing situation than are those in the central provinces of Canada/ and so, Mr. Speaker, I would like at this time to devote a few moments to dealing with some of the problems confronting Canada generally but affecting particularly the people of British Columbia, -who to-day are faced not only with the possibility of attack but also with the problem of a resident Japanese population totalling, according to the recent registration, 23,461. First of all, I want to assure the house of my desire to be fair and tolerant in all I have to say in connection with the Japanese dwelling within our country, and I should like to point out that sc far I have endeavoured to refrain from making any public statements which might in any way incite racial feelings amongst our own people, realizing, apart entirely from a sense of common justice to the Japanese, how dangerous such feelings might become, realizing also that one had to remember that many Canadian citizens were still living in Japan, likewise the fact that numbers of Canadian soldiers were prisoners of war at the hands of the Japanese in Hong Kong.
First of all, let me commend the government for the speedy action it took, following the declaration of war with Japan, of ordering every Japanese fishing boat to be taken into custody. Over, 1,100 boats have been collected by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the naval authorities, close to 900 of these boats being moored in the Fraser river at New Westminster.
While it would only be fair to say that the standing committee appointed by the government did some good work, in conjunction with

The Address

Mr. Reid
officials of the external affairs department and others, under the chairmanship of the hon. Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), it was unfortunate, I believe, that members of parliament from British Columbia, particularly members from the coast districts, had not been consulted in the matter. It was certainly strange that their advice was not sought on such an important matter.
The government is perhaps not so much to blame as are some of the Ottawa officials in the government service who, it would appear, were determined to ignore any advice or help from the people's elected representatives, who are more aware of the facts of the situation than were most, if not all, of these officials.
May I say to the government that the decision not to issue any fishing licences to the Japanese was well received by the people of British Columbia; but no sooner had it become known that the Japanese fishing fleet was being taken into custody and that no fishing licences would be issued to Japanese for the duration of the war, than representations were made by certain interested parties asking for the release of the boats to the Japanese again.

speechtext: Who were those interested parties?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, I can name one. My information is that the head of British Columbia Packers, Limited, who is also chairman of the wartime merchant shipping board, was one who was very active.
I want to warn the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) against what I believe might happen under the present policy whereby all Japanese are being allowed to sell their individual boats. These boats are worth from eight hundred to five or six thousand dollars, according to the size and class of boat; and any sales made, so we understand, must be on a strictly cash basis. The fleet consists of about eleven hundred vessels, and worth, in the aggregate, between two and three million dollars. It is hardly likely that all of these boats will be sold, especially when actual cash for them has to be found, and so we might again witness some of the fish packing companies acquiring ownership, through finance, of large numbers of these boats and, with this ownership of both boats and fishing' gear, largely controlling the fishing industry in British Columbia. This is at least what happened in the past and, it is to be hoped, will not be allowed to happen again.
It has been intimated that the government intend to move certain numbers of able-bodied male Japanese between certain ages only, and from certain designated military areas. The
age limit proposed is between that of eighteen and forty-five years. What the designated military areas are to be has not yet been made known publicly. My advice would be, if the government is going to move every ablebodied male Japanese citizen, not to leave any over the age of forty-five; and further, the entire British Columbia coast as well as Vancouver island, Queen Charlotte and other islands should be military prohibited districts for the Japanese and enemy aliens. Considerable concern is felt in British Columbia concerning where the government intends removing the able-bodied Japanese to, and I believe most people in British Columbia would agree with the statement that no community in British Columbia really wants them. One suggestion would be that in view of the shortage of farm labour in Ontario and other eastern provinces, the government send three or four thousand east and so provide farmers in the central and eastern provinces with all the farm help they require. This would save considerable expense to the country compared with the proposed scheme of road work in British Columbia whereby the government proposes to pay them for this -work. The people of Ontario, especially round Ottawa, and other provinces have always evinced a more kindly feeling towards these people than the people of British Columbia. We in that province would not mind their departure. I feel sure that if they leave British Columbia, there is one song we would not sing, and that is that splendid old Jacobite song, once sung for Prince Charlie, and now sung when dear friends are departing, "Will ye no come back again?"
The problem of the Japanese in Canada has been principally one of British Columbia's problems, and one which should never have occurred but for the action of the federal government in days long past. From information which we have it would appear that in the year 1894 Great Britain concluded a commercial or trade treaty with Japan. It was simply a treaty for trade purposes only, but one of the clauses of that treaty was to allow Japanese citizens to enter, travel or reside. This particular clause did not affect Great Britain, and at that time she had little interest as to whether the Japanese settled in the British colonies or not. Objection to the clause was made by Australia, so Great Britain offered to negotiate a new trade treaty without a clause of this kind being inserted, and restricting the entry of Japanese nationals into the various countries of the self-governing colonies. Canada preferred to accept the clause as it stood; Australia would not. The acceptance by Canada of that clause in a

The Address-Mr. Reid

trade treaty has been a most unfortunate one for British Columbia, and I believe for Canada generally, for the people of that province have had forced on them an unassimilable race of people, who cannot in the strict sense become truly Canadians. The people of British Columbia have long been protesting to Ottawa against the peaceful penetration of the Japanese in that province, but all protests have been of little avail. In fact, apart from some changes made in the gentleman's agreement from time to time, our appeals to the federal government have been met with almost complete indifference.
At one stage of our history British Columbia endeavoured to emulate Australia, which country successfully defied the attempts of Great Britain to force the entry of orientals on them, but the action of British Columbia was vetoed at Ottawa. It is well known that the pressure of certain Montreal financial interests had something to do with the matter, for back in those years they wanted to have plenty of cheap labour on tap, especially in British Columbia.
There are no doubt many loyal Japanese in Canada, but who can tell the loyal ones from the others? Would anyone say regarding any of our missionaries, or of other Canadians of British stock who have lived from upwards of twenty to sixty years in Japan, as some of them have done, that after living there all those years they or their children born in Japan would be now more loyal to Japan than to Canada or Britain? Of course they would not. Then why assert, as some do, that the Japanese are any different in this regard than our own or other races would be? I am not finding any fault with them in this regard. I am merely reciting what is, after all, only a natural human characteristic and which would seem to be part of the make-up of man and woman in almost every race.
Another fact w'hich should be mentioned here is, why have so many of the Canadian-born Japanese gone back to Japan to complete or carry out their military training in that country? Contrary to what one would imagine or expect from Canadian-born children of certain foreign races in this country, and which is not generally known, many of our so-called new Canadians born in this country are more intensely nationalistic for their parents' homeland than are the parents themselves, and this applies to many of the university class of Japanese born and educated in British Columbia. Do not forget that almost all of them are registered in Japan even though born in Canada and that Japan looks upon them as still being her nationals.

The trouble to my mind with many people- and this includes many round Ottawa-is that they refuse to face the facts on this oriental question. Personally I see no great hope of a permanent solution for the Japanese question in British Columbia other than by way of repatriation.
Perhaps the question would not be so great and might partly be solved were the Japanese spread out over the entire nine provinces. But as the policy seems to have been for the Japanese to congregate almost entirely in one province, the problem in that province becomes a very great and .perplexing one. I would, however, treat all. Japanese in this country fairly and without hatred. Remember, when we speak of repatriation we should think in terms of the future, looking towards the solution of a better and more united Canada. It is worth noting here that Russia, that country from which much can be learned to-day, took action immediately Germany attacked her and removed some 387,000 persons of German descent whose forbears had lived in Russia as far back as 1817. Russia believed, "once a German always a German," and removed every last one of them, lock, stock and barrel, to Siberia.^
With regard to the Japanese situation, if wise steps are not taken now to deal with the problem, looking towards a satisfactory solution, the problem will be an ever-recurring and contentious one, and it is my plea now to the government that it should be dealt with in the light of British Columbia's experience rather than, as in the past, from an entirely -Ottawa and far-away point of view.

Well it should be. Coming back to the remarks I have to make regarding the war in the Pacific, it is evident now that Japan fooled the allies prior to December, 1941, in her war with China, making them believe she was not as strong as she really was. It is interesting to note that both Russia and Japan adopted a like policy in relation to their military strength and preparedness; for it is evident now that Stalin put it al. over Hitler regarding the strength of Russia. Japan, using similar tactics, hid her real military strength from the rest of the world in preparation for her fight against the United States and Great Britain, both of which countries she is endeavouring with all her military might to drive out of the Pacific. My prayer is that our war cabinet and high military command will accept these statements about the Pacific situation more seriously than they seem to have done in the past, and in speaking as I have about this matter, I do so

The Address-Mr. Hlynka
because I feel it to be my duty, and to warn the government and the country against the possible danger which I believe exists. We on the Pacific coast would like to see in all important centres more anti-aircraft guns, searchlights and other military defence measures. The people on the Pacific coast, however, are not asking the impossible and are well aware of the enormous demands for military equipment of every kind which is urgently required to-day to meet the enemy in all the widely flung battle fronts. I urge the Minister of National Defence, for whom I have the greatest regard, that when he speaks he tell us, as frankly as the situation will allow, of the steps which have been taken for the protection of the British Columbia coast. In the light of the actual war situation as it exists to-day, we do .not expect him to reveal any military information which might help the enemy or jeopardize the safety of our people, but we do ask that he take us into his confidence as far as deemed advisable, believing that a frank statement of the situation will be of inestimable help, looking towards the prevention of any possible war hysteria or panic which might arise.
I have one suggestion to make in closing. It is that the minister bring back General McNaughton from England and have him inspect the defences of both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, and in the light of his experience advise the government in connection with the defence of Canada against possible invasion. General McNaughton has been in England now for some considerable time and not only has witnessed enemy air attacks and bombardments but is in the unique position of knowing what the actual fortifications are in Great Britain against invasion either from the sea or from the air. He is fully conversant also with modern military tactics to be employed against- the enemy should invasion arise. He has first-hand experience, information and knowledge such as few of the military staff in Canada possess. General McNaughton is the most experienced man we have for advice on how modern warfare should be conducted, and apart altogether from the respect in which he is held in Great Britain, the fact that prior to the fall of Dunkirk he stood out against allowing Canadian troops to go to France because of the lack of adequate mechanical military equipment, show's the calibre of this general, who merits, I believe, the thanks of all Canadians.
It is my opinion that if something like this were done, and any recommendations made were carried out, it would not only allay to quite a considerable extent, the fears of many
of our people but also have the effect of placing us in a better position to repel any possible invasion or attack from air or sea on either the Atlantic or the Pacific coasts.
In closing, may I say that like every hon. member I realize the seriousness of war conditions to-day, and so have endeavoured in my remarks to be as fair and tolerant as possible, trusting, how'ever, that some attention will be given by the government to the suggestions made with regard to the problems I now bring to their attention.
