Mr. Speaker, during the past two sessions of the present parliament our task has been directed toward a solution of the problems which confront us in our national life, particularly those which arise in the prosecution of the war. Considerable progress has been made in this initial period, but no effort could have been too great while the destiny of free peoples was at stake. From now on, and until a decisive victory is ultimately won, both on the battlefields and at the peace conferences, not only must we further mobilize, equip and maintain our armed forces as our chief contribution to the cause of freedom, but we must of necessity go beyond this primary requisite.
We must not only -win the war, but we must also make certain that we shall win the peace. To achieve less would be to fail in the trust bestowed upon us, the sacred privilege of delivering to future generations the hard-won liberties of our forefathers. It is our duty, therefore, to study and prevent the weaknesses and recurring dangers of past adjustments-or, shall I say, the lack of proper adjustments-of world problems which gave rise to the present world conflagration. This should be one of our many immediate concerns.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members will agree with me when I say that we are faced to-day with problems of first magnitude. Many of these problems have arisen with the present conflict, but multitudes of them find root in the past. We cannot, therefore, shirk responsibility in the solution of this chaotic state of affairs. World problems are our problems; for they have either a direct or an indirect bearing upon our national life-yes, even upon our individual lives.
The Address-Mr. Hlynka

We must necessarily realize that it is not the war alone that we are fighting to-day; we find ourselves also in the grip of two of the greatest revolutions of all time. Nationally we are fighting a war; internally and internationally we are engaged in two prodigious revolutions-one economic, one political. We are therefore endeavouring to survive one of the most critical and dangerous of transitional periods.
Let us, then, examine the role that we Canadians are playing in this struggle, and let us envision the role that Canada is destined to play in the future.
AAre are now in the third year of war. To what extent have we crystallized our views on Canada's foreign policy? What plans are we prepared to advance or adopt as the basis for post-war reorganization and1 reconstruction of the world? How many hours have we devoted in this chamber to the discussion of this problem during the last two years? If none, why not? Can we afford to be caught unprepared in this respect? For, as we know, this war will also end sooner or later as all other wars are supposed to have ended.
Now, when we consider the position that Canada occupies among the nations of the world at this time, it does seem that we have underestimated her importance. As a matter of fact, until recently Canada's position was unique in that it was second only to that of Great Britain; indeed in many respects, even with the entry of the United States into the conflict, Canada still remains a number one ally of Great Britain. I say that with all due respect and consideration to the material aid given to Great Britain by our good neighbour directly to the south of us, and with all due respect and consideration to the entry of the Soviet Union into this conflict on our side.
To amplify my statement: Canada's strategic position makes her the logical mediator between Great Britain and the United States. Her geographical location makes her an ideal arsenal for the turning out of tools of war for the allies. She is admirably situated for the training fields of the empire forces, and especially the empire air training plan. And lastly, because of her limitless potential natural resources and her vast, rich wheat fields, she will undoubtedly be the key to post-war reconstruction of Britain. It is only fitting, therefore, that Canada's foreign policy should be commensurate with her important position.
It is gratifying indeed to find that the broad principles which are intended as the basis for post-war reorganization of the world have been enunciated. I refer, of course, to the now historic Atlantic charter, proclaimed by two of the world's men of destiny-the

Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Church-hill, and the President of the United States, Mr. Roosevelt. I am more than pleased, Mr. Speaker, to hear reference made to the Atlantic charter in the speech from the throne.
Then again, there are the four great human freedoms proclaimed by the President of the United States-freedom of speech and expression, freedom of every person to worship God in his own way, freedom from want and freedom from fear.
These declarations deserve all the acclaim they have already received from all parts of the world, particularly for their universality and noble purpose. We, of course, welcome and accept these principles just as we had accepted the fourteen points of President Wilson after the last war. AVe may be proud at least of the fact that the democratic world recognizes that world stability and enduring peace can be achieved only on the basis of freedom of all peoples capable of shaping and directing their own destinies.
Further, in his address of January 6, 1941, President Roosevelt had this to say on the subject:
No lasting peace can be bought at the expense of other peoples' freedom.
Again, in his speech delivered at the annual dinner of the AVhite House Correspondents' Association, he said:
Humanity will never permanently accept a system imposed by conquest and based on Slavery.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, not only are these statements true, but they are expressions of foresight and vision. We can no longer tolerate a short-sighted plan or settlement. There must be built a new world citadel of freedom and civilization. If we ever hope to have stability and enduring peace, the principles of freedom must constantly be kept in mind and incorporated into the post-war settlement. If this basis is ignored, let us then not expect a peaceful world in the immediate future; the lives spent in this and the last war will then have been given in vain.
Let us look a step further. Should not the democracies, of imperative necessity, formulate a more definite and detailed set of proposals which will give the needed promise of release to all peoples under the domination of the aggressor nations? Should not our proposals be more positive, more dynamic, so that they may add more inspiration to the explosive force of the temporarily subdued peoples? I venture to suggest that in this manner we would change the whole course of the war very much more in our favour. I make this observation because it can well be

The Address

Mr. Hlynka
assumed that the axis powers are bound to offer some enticing formula to subdued nations for the express purpose of giving themselves a breathing moment before they begin tightening the reins on those unfortunate countries. Germany is already trying desperately to consolidate her position in the overrun regions. She is organizing these areas into zones which are to operate in complete subordination to her, and she is totally ignoring all racial and ethnographic lines. It is a sort of forced federal union. It would mean an eventual and permanent enslavement of millions of people. It would become a new and horrible prison of nations.
In view of this increasingly dangerous threat, the allies should, therefore, take it upon themselves to become the guardians of sovereign ideals and sovereign nations. Can we not promise all of them their national sovereignty, which would be in accordance with the spirit of the Atlantic charter, and which would make a revolutionary rebellion on their part worth while? It would be an inspiration and a challenge to them. For, as we know, there is no stronger force and incentive than that manifest in the defence of personal and national existence. I cannot, therefore, emphasize too strongly the immediate need on the part of democracies to make known their foreign policy in as complete and definite form as time and conditions permit. The issues at stake are too important for us not to make use of the incentive of confidence in the future-instead of vague hopes and wishful thinking.
Allow me now to draw your attention to the three items relevant to national sovereignty as outlined in the Atlantic charter. They are points 2, 3 and 6. Here is what they say:
Second, they desire to see no territorial changes that do not accord with the freely expressed wishes of the people concerned.
Third, they respect the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live; and they wish to see sovereign rights and self-government restored to those who have been forcibly deprived of them.
Sixth, after the final destruction of the nazi tyranny, they hope to see established a peace which will afford to all nations the means of dwelling in safety within their own boundaries, and which will afford assurance that all the men in all the lands may live out their lives in freedom from fear and want.
These three points deal generally with the phase of the problem which I am discussing. They read well, but I found numerous interpretations of them. One outstanding United States publication interprets the Atlantic charter as being opposed to the setting up of any new organisms. Of course, much depends
on how the word "new" is interpreted. But are we to understand that nations who were not fortunate enough to liberate themselves during the last war shall remain in bondage? More clarification of this point is definitely needed. Then, again, the charter was interpreted as favouring the federal union proposals. Personally, I fail to find in the document any trace of expression of these views. As a matter of fact I find that the charter upholds the sovereignty of all peoples in accordance with their expressed will, which is definitely contrary to ideas propounded by federal unionists.
From what I have said thus far, it is evident that this question of foreign relations policy is an extremely broad one in scope. I wish, therefore, to confine my following remarks specifically to the discussion of a Ukrainian independent state and its importance to the British commonwealth of nations.
The question may arise in the minds of some hon. members as to why should we Canadians be interested in an independent Ukrainian state in Europe. Is it because Ukrainian-Canadians constitute a large group of our citizens, and we owe them that courtesy? Is it because they are so generously enlisting in great numbers in the Canadian armed forces and are ready to give their lives for Canada? Is it because of the heroic contribution of Ukrainians on the battlefields of the Ukraine against Germany? Or, is it because it is in the very blood of the English-speaking people always to stand up for the rights of others as well as their own? Yes, but there is a much more important reason than those I have already given.
Above all, a Ukrainian independent state in eastern Europe would be important to the British commonwealth of nations and the United States as a balance of power. I venture to suggest that in the not distant future the British people and the principles for which they stand will be more closely ' associated with the Ukrainians than they have ever been before.
Furthermore, Ukraine is important because of the extent of its territory, the richness of its natural resources, the size of its population, and its strategic position with reference to the Black sea, the Dardanelles, Iran, Iraq, 1 the Persian gulf and India. Professor G. W. Simpson, of Saskatchewan university, has this to say in his "Atlas of History and Geography of the Ukraine":
Thus the Ukraine constitutes a wide assembling place which could be used either by ambitious dictators as the starting point for sweeping military conquest, or by wise statesmen as a strong wedge-like area of defence which would stabilize all these regions tributary to the Black sea.
The Address-Mr. Hlynka

Consequently, it is definitely contrary to the interests of Britain to permit Germany to take and hold the Ukraine and exploit its people and its resources for aggrandizement and greater power. Again, it would not be in the best interests of Britain to see any other power enslave the Ukrainian people and, with the use of their territory and natural resources, become a dominant power holding this strategic position in eastern Europe.
Finally, a division of the territory after the fashion of the division made after the last war would only complicate the problems of Europe, and the dangerous situation would remain unchanged. Hence the problem of a Ukrainian independent state in eastern Europe is of extreme importance to the British commonwealth of nations and to the stability of the world.
I have before me a handbook prepared under the authority of the historic section of the British foreign office, entitled "The Ukraine", the topic which I propose to discuss briefly. This booklet is numbered 52 of the series of such authoritative information prepared and collected for the sole purpose of having this information available for those who were to participate in the peace conferences. It may be observed from the series number that there must have been at least fifty-one others of the kind, dealing with various important problems. This booklet contains information having to do with physical geography, political history, social and political conditions, and much other useful material. One cannot help but admire the British for their thoroughness in dealing with important matters such as these; on the other hand, the total lack of similar preparation on our part in Canada stands out in striking contrast.
True, many Canadians show a keen interest in the Ukrainian problem. Many of them seek information on the subject, but it is essential that they obtain their information from authoritative and unbiased sources. All those interested in the subject must remember that there is a great deal of distorted information emanating from people who are not totally disinterested in the possession and the control of the Ukraine. This information is usually disseminated with the purpose of obliterating the authenticity of the ethnological and ethnographical existence of the Ukrainian people. For example, any aspiration manifested by Ukrainians looking to freedom and independence in their own native land is immediately given the interpretation of being instigated by an enemy of the British. This method of propaganda is by no means new, but unless one guards against such sources of information he may be hopelessly misled.

For the benefit of those who may be interested in the subject I wish to place on record just a few authoritative sources of information: "Ukraine, an Atlas of its History and Geography," by G. W. Simpson, professor of European history, university of Saskatchewan, published in 1941; "History of the Ukraine," by D. Doroshenko. professor of Prague and Warsaw universities, which was edited by Professor Simpson, and published in 1939. The third and perhaps the most comprehensive study is "A History of Ukraine," by Michael Hrushevsky, one of the world's outstanding historians. This book was edited by 0. J. Frederiksen, professor of history at Miami university, and published by Yale university press in 1941.
May I now give this house, so far as my humble ability will permit, the fundamental facts concerning Ukraine and the Ukrainian people? First let me deal with the land they inhabit and claim.
Ukraine is a vast rich territory lying in the southeastern corner of Europe on the threshold of Asia, immediately north of the Black sea. It is the second largest ethnographic territory in Europe and fourteenth largest in the world. This territory comprises 362,200 square miles.
Immediately prior to the last world war the whole Ukraine was held by Russia and Austro-Hungary.
By 1923 the Ukraine was dismembered and divided among the four neighbouring nations. The largest portion, comprising 298,610 square miles and containing 35,026,000 Ukrainians, called the Great Ukraine, was assigned to Russia, and was incorporated as one of the republics of the Soviet Union. The western Ukraine, comprising 51,042 square miles and containing 7,500,000 Ukrainians, was made a Polish "protectorate". The provinces of Bessarabia and Bukovina, comprising 6,795 squaremilesand containing 1,500,000 Ukrainians, was placed under Roumanian rule, while Carpatho-Ukraine, comprising 5,753 square miles and containing 600,000 Ukrainians, was assigned to Czechoslovakia.
At the moment almost the entire territory has become the battlefield of the German and the Soviet Union forces. It has been for many months and still is being torn by destructive forces of war, and the Ukrainian people are undergoing the most cruel ordeal of their history. In addition to this tragic fate that befell the Ukrainian people, the scorched earth policy of the Soviet government was mainly applied to the Ukraine. The land which is capable of providing freedom and life to its people has brought nothing but extreme tragedy, with slavery and death.

The Address-Mr. Hlynka
To one who has not the facts about the Ukraine it may seem confusing why so many nations are forever determined to grab a piece of this land for themselves. The answer is that it is one of the richest regions in the entire world. Ukraine is often referred to as the granary of Europe. It is more than that. Her mineral deposits are the envy of all her good neighbours. The 1932 Encyclopaedia Americana points out that in 1928-29 Ukraine supplied the Soviet Union with 80 per cent of its coal, 60 per cent of its iron, 95 per cent of its manganese, 80 per cent of its sugar, the bulk of its wheat, vast quantities of mercury, copper and gold. The striking fact is that its rightful owners share little in this wealth.
There are now in the neighbourhood of 50 million Ukrainians in the world. Numerically they are the third largest group in Europe and ninth largest in the world. They first appeared in history in the fourth century. My time will not permit me to deal with the ethnology and the general characteristics of the people at this time; suffice it to say that C. S. Coon, professor of anthropology at Harvard university, states in his book, "Races of Europe," that Ukrainians are a distinct and separate people.
Perhaps the greatest contribution made by Ukrainians to the world was that of staving off the Asiatic hordes for many centuries from invading Europe. That is what Lord Tweedsmuir meant when he said on September 21, 1936, at Fraserwood, Manitoba, "for it was your race which for centuries held the southeastern gate of Europe against the attacks from the east."
Again, it was through Kiev, the capital of the Ukraine, that Christianity was introduced into eastern Europe in 988. Let me mention one or two other contributions in art, music, and literature. Alexander Archipenko, one of the world's foremost contemporary sculptors, now living in the United States, is a Ukrainian. The immortal Tschaikowsky, in the field of music, was of Ukrainian origin. Taras Shevchenko, the Robert Burns of the Slavic races, was a Ukrainian. These are but a few indications of Ukrainian contributions to the world.
When national states were established after the last world war it was held that the basis accepted was not some remote appeal to historic claims, but rather a clear and unmistakable determination of the people to rule themselves. With regard to the historic claims of many peoples, some, like Finland, had not known complete political independence for many centuries; some, like Esthonia, had never known political independence in the modern sense of the word.
The Ukraine, however, has had a continuous historic tradition extending back for over a 44561-16
thousand years, and three timefc, at least, this tradition incorporated itself in terms of political independence. First, there was the Kievan state, existing from the ninth to the middle of the fourteenth century; then the Cossack state, established in 1648, which lasted to the middle of the eighteenth century, and lastly, the United Ukrainian Republic of 1918-23.
At the time when Alfred the Great Of England was attempting to maintain his Saxon state against the Danes, the ancestors of the Ukrainian people were establishing a large and flourishing kingdom with its centre at Kiev. This Kievan state, with its Slav-Byzantine culture, was the outstanding political state in eastern Europe. It is the fountainhead of the Ukrainian historical tradition. When it disintegrated into principalities and suffered, the devastating blow of the Tartar invasion its traditions lived on in the southern principalities, particularly in the western Ukraine. Although the western Ukraine fell to Poland and the other principalities to Lithuania, which was later joined to Poland, the ancient Ukrainian laws, customs and language persisted and developed.
Again when Oliver Cromwell in England, in the seventeenth century, was striking a mighty blow for that liberty which we are to-day defending, Bohdan Khmelnitsky created on the basis of Ukrainian tradition a free and independent Cossack state. Unfortunately Khmelnitsky had not the advantage of a sea wrall, which Cromwell enjoyed, and the state which he had erected was torn between Poland and the rising state of Muscovy which was then becoming the modern empire of Russia. So firmly entrenched, however, were the institutions of self-government in the Ukraine, that it was more than a hundred years after the death of Khmelnitsky, in the latter half of the eighteenth century, before the imperialist regime could root out the last remnants of these institutions of selfgovernment.
But the love of freedom which is an undying part of the human spirit was again awakened in the nineteenth century among the Ukrainian people as well as among the Czechs, the Poles and others who had been suppressed.
Finally, in the first world war, when the Russian empire fell, then from its ruins, for the third time in the history of the Ukrainian people, there emerged a Ukrainian independent state, proclaimed on January 22, 1918. Nine months later the Austro-Hungarian empire fell, and from its remnants there was created the Western Ukrainian National Republic, proclaimed on the first day of November, 1918, ten days before the armistice. These

The Address-Mr. Hlynka

two Ukrainian areas were proclaimed united on Januar3'- 22, 1919, forming a United Ukrainian Republic.
The Ukrainian patriots fought desperately to defend this state so -that they might live as free people among other nations of the world. They lost this freedom, and one element in their misfortune was the fact that their cause was so gravely misunderstood and misrepresented. By 1923 the Ukrainians found themselves divided among four states, as I have already pointed out.
It seemed that it was the original intention of the Paris peace conference to give the Ukrainians the right of self-determination in the western Ukraine. In 1923, however, the Council of Ambassadors granted to Poland the title to this area, on the distinct understanding that she would eventually grant autonomy to this part of the Ukraine under the stipulated clauses of the Minorities treaty of 1919. Finally, in 1934, Poland formally repudiated this obligation.
The results of these minorities treaties present many interesting angles. It may be granted that it was not easy to divide the territory in question into national states, since there were many conflicting claims; but, allowing even for that, all were not treated with equal consideration. For instance, in the territorial revision after the last war some eleven states were created' that were not on the map in 1914. Some of these were: Poland, with some 20 millions of people; Yugoslavia, with about 15 millions; Finland, with 3,600,000; Lithuania, with 2,500,000; Latvia, with 2,000,000, and Esthonia, with 1,100,000. I strongly uphold the granting of sovereign rights to all these nations, because I am a firm believer in the sovereign rights of all peoples in accordance with their will. It does seem inconsistent, however, that Ukrainians, with over 40 millions at that time, came out of the struggle empty-handed, in spite of the fact that they had been an historic unit in the past. Were not the Ukrainians entitled to the same privilege as others? If not, why not?
Another error in the settlement arose out of the fact that minorities created by this division constituted a dangerously high percentage. According to Mr. C. A. Macartney, a recognized authority on European affairs, in Czechoslovakia thirty-three per cent were other than Czechs or Slovaks; in Poland over twenty-five per cent were non-Polish; in Roumania over twenty-five per cent were other than Roumanians. The important question is, can we afford to ignore racial lines in the future?
CMr. Hlynka.]
The present collapse of the state structure in Europe has again involved the Ukrainian people, along with other peoples, in utmost misery and desolatiou at the hands of the aggressor nations. The Ukrainians have again joined hands with other liberty-loving peoples in a fight for freedom. In Carpatho-Ukraine they fought against the axis partner, Hungary, in 1938. In western Ukraine and in Poland they fought against Germany in 1939, and they are now fighting against Germany with the Soviet Union forces.
Ukrainians fought for their freedom throughout their long and tragic history. They fight for it now, and they will continue to fight for it until they are free. Ukrainians believe that they are just as much entitled to their sovereign rights as any other people are; they wish to contribute their maximum share to culture and civilization of the world. This will be possible only through the restoration of their own independence. A nation can give its best only when free from bondage. These are the tenets of the Atlantic charter; these are the tenets of Christian civilization.
It may be pointed out by some that there appear to be two obstacles in the way of realization of Ukrainian sovereignty. In the first place it may be suggested that after .this war there will be no sovereign states; that some sort of federal union will take their place. Personally I do not believe that the British people would favour any plan that would require the forfeiture of their sovereignty. If they did, they would not be fighting this war.
The second obstacle which may be suggested is one with reference to the Soviet Union. It may be said that, since the Soviet Union is our ally in this war, any suggestion of an independent Ukraine might endanger our relations with the Soviet Union. Let me remind hon. members that, according to press reports, the Soviet government favours the proposals embodied in the Atlantic charter. That this is so, was indicated by the British Foreign Secretary, Mr. Eden, after his recent return from Moscow. In addition to that, article 17 of the Soviet Union constitution (1936) says that "Each union republic is reserved the right freely to secede from the U.S.S.R." This should be sufficient assurance that the Soviet Union would be inclined to favour a recognition of the principle of the sovereignty of nations.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to leave with the house the following suggestion. In view of the fact that all the subdued countries that had been sovereign nations prior to this war are now privileged to form their provisional governments in exile

The Address-Mr. Bradette
in order that they may carry on the work in the interests of their respective peoples, and in view of the fact that Ukrainians, who form a larger group than any of these, have not now that privilege simply because they were not an independent nation immediately prior to this war, I humbly submit that steps should be taken by the allied governments to make it possible for the Ukrainians to be represented at the various conferences now being held from time to time. In Great Britain, the United States and Canada, there are in existence United Ukrainian committees, whose primary object is to assist the governments in Britain, the United States and Canada in the successful prosecution of the war. I do suggest, if I may, sir, that since all the allied nations are fighting for a common cause of freedom, that Ukrainian committees to which I have referred be also invited to delegate their representative or representatives to express the view of 50 million Ukrainian people at conferences held by the allied nations.
I believe I have sufficiently pointed out that the stability of Europe and of the world can be achieved only on the basis of universal justice. The European madhouse will remain a madhouse until Europe is reconstructed with freedom written into every word of its constitution. When that is done we may expect a lasting peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with my remarks I want to compliment the previous speaker, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) upon presenting so lucidly and forcibly one of the great problems which his people living in Europe are facing now, and which we shall have to face and try to solve after the present conflict is over.
It is with a certain amount of trepidation, realizing that all hon. members are alive to the seriousness of the situation, that I dare to speak on this occasion. I believe, however, that this is the time, in the course of the debate on the speech from the throne, as the floor of this House of Commons is the place, for a member of parliament occasionally to express his sentiments on great matters which are agitating public opinion.
I was not here when the mover (Mr. Fournier, Hull) and the seconder (Mr. Macdonald, Brantford City) spoke, but I made it a point to read their speeches, and I join with others in complimenting them sincerely upon the splendid presentation they made. I also listened attentively to the excellent address given by that true Canadian, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) last week, and I might say the same about the speeches given 44561-16*
by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell) and the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Blackmore).
There is one feeling that, I am sure, animates this house. We are all in agreement on the fact that a total war effort is desirable at this time and until full victory has been attained. We all want to do everything we possibly can to prosecute the war successfully. One party may think differently from another with regard to certain phases of our activities, but surely it is possible in the present serious situation, in this critical time in our Canadian history and of the world, for us all to get our hearts and minds together and bring about unity in our own ranks so that we may forge ahead successfully with our war effort.
Let me address sincere felicitations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). In my opinion he gave a splendid, illuminating address, and I hope it will be possible for every Canadian to read, to scrutinize and carefully to analyse that speech. The Prime Minister showed what we have done in prosecuting this war. He made it known to the Canadian people, to the people of the British empire, and to all the people of the civilized world that we in Canada are willing to go further than we have gone and to make still greater efforts, and sacrifices, in time, energy and wealth in order to preserve -all those things that Canadians cherish. There is one thing that surprises me-I have wondered at it ever since the war began-and that is the fact that many members' of parliament find it possible to say, generally speaking, that Canadians do not realize the seriousness of the situation. Indeed, some hon. gentlemen go as far as to say that the Canadian people did not realize the situation at the time of the election in 1940. I suggest that anyone who has read at all carefully the history of the first great war, from 1914 to 1918, as well as some military works depicting not only the horrors of that war, but the horrors of the war which historians at that time foresaw would take place in the future, in other words, the war in which we are at present engaged; anyone who listened at all carefully to some of the speeches that were delivered at that time in the House of Commons by such men as General Ross, who represented Kingston, and who gave so vividly, from personal knowledge, accounts of what had taken place in the last war, and predicted what might happen in the future, does not rate the intelligence of Canadians very high if he stands up in this forum and declares that the Canadian people to-day do not realize, or did not realize, at the time of the election in 1940,
The Address-Mr. Bradette

the seriousness of this war. Our people knew and know of the meaning of this horrible conflict. We all knew how serious it would be. We could not help realizing it after Germany had conquered Poland in a few weeks. We knew what was in store for all the freedom-loving democracies unless we prepared ourselves accordingly.
I protest against this attitude on the part of certain people. There is scarcely a Canadian family that has not some representative in active service on the European side, and if for no other reason that that, I am sure we are all fully conscious of the gravity of the situation and the necessity for combining all our energies so that we may make sure that we shall be absolutely victorious.
May I say a few words now about the plebiscite? I represent a riding in which there are all the nationalities known to the civilized world. Ever since the total war movement started, I have been receiving letters, in some of which I have been definitely told that unless I am absolutely for conscription I should resign. As far as I am personally concerned, let me say that on this important question I shall follow primarily the dictates of my own conscience and what I believe to be in the interests of my own country and of the British empire. I will not be led astray, or I will not be led one way or the other, by other considerations. I believe that every member of parliament must accept responsibility not only for his own political actions, but, to a large extent, for some leadership in his own constituency, and advance his ideas earnestly [DOT] and sincerely.
Before coming to this session I was sincerely convinced that this government had done almost as well as it could do under the circumstances. I believed that it was fully aware of the situation, notwithstanding that in the last three or four months there has been a vicious attack from a small section of the country', of which attack of necessity parliament must be cognizant. I am absolutely in favour of holding a plebiscite at this time, and my chief reason is this. I think that when we read the history of Canada we realize that at all times we have, had reason to believe implicitly in the fairmindedness, the logic and the intelligence of Canadian voters, and they always realized and accepted the fullness of their responsibilities.
Some members of the opposition this afternoon criticized severely the fact that the plebiscite would cost some money. If I mistake not, I heard almost the same sort of criticism a few months ago about national registration, and only a year ago, before the

census was taken, there was a section of the press as well as of the opposition deploring the fact that the government was going to spend money on a census. Everyone now realizes that it is of national service. I do not wish to assume the role of prophet, but I suggest that when the history of this particular episode which we are now discussing comes to be written, the general feeling will be that the government acted rightly in asking the people to pronounce upon this important question.
I have not time to go over the achievements of Canada in this war. Any Canadian who wishes to get the facts can find them not only in the speech delivered by the Prime Minister at the beginning of the session, but in the press of the country. The Canadian achievement has been little short of miraculous. I am the last man to suggest that everything has been done exactly as it should have been done, or that we have done all that we could possibly have done. But we have learned a good deal from the last war; we are learning in this war too, and I have no doubt whatever that our activities wrill be greater as we go on.
Some of our colleagues on the other side seem to make light of the promise with regard to conscription that was given to the Canadian people in the election of 1940. In my constituency, which w'as typical of 244 others, conscription was not an issue, for the simple reason that I as Liberal candidate, my opponent Mr. Crumb, the Conservative, and Mr. Teeple, the Labour candidate, were all in agreement, and decidedly so, that conscription of man-power for service overseas should not bo implemented in this parliament. We have to render an account of our stewardship on that question, and our position in this regard has not changed since 1940. I believe that our young men would always answer to the call of duty voluntarily wherever their services would be required.
Let me quote what was said by Doctor Manion, who became leader of the Conservative party in the last election, on the floor of the House of Commons on March 30, 1939, as reported at page 2440:
In the last war the conscription of men to go to the front caused violent racial antagonisms, much disharmony, bitterness and misunderstanding-conditions from which as yet we have not wholly recovered; and on top of that I believe I am expressing the opinion of authorities when I say that it was of no real military value so far as the empire was concerned.
That statement was repeated on the floor of the house. Doctor Manion stated that as far

The Address-Mr. Bradette
as he could ascertain, only 10,000 men at the most got into the fighting line. He went on to say:
The policy that I suggest is the one which I gave three days ago in an interview: First, that there should be no conscription of Canadians to serve outside the borders of Canada; second, that we should have full cooperation with the British empire short of the conscription of men to serve outside our borders.
Of this I never heard any contradiction from the Conservative party. That was prior to an election. Perhaps there was some personal reason for Doctor Manion making such a statement. But we had an election during 1940, and in the city, of Quebec during the campaign Doctor Manion, addressing a very large meeting, faced a large banner on which was written:
I am absolutely opposed to conscription.
These are the words of Doctor Manion concerning that great issue on that occasion:
I stated on March 30, 1939, just about a year ago, in the House of Commons, that I was opposed to conscription because of its failure in the last war-
Mark you, "failure" is the word he used. -and because it had stirred up misunderstanding and strife in our country when the duty of our public men is to hold this country together, rather than to break it up. I have not waited until I came to the province of Quebec to make this statement. I made it a month ago at Brockville in the opening speech of my campaign. '
When I read the report of that meeting, the newspapers were all in agreement that it was a wonderful omen of Conservative victory. He continued:
I have made it more than twenty times since then in almost every speech which I have delivered as far west as Victoria, B.C. Thus I have set forth my attitude in five provinces of Canada before coming to Quebec, and I state here again to-night that I am against conscription, and that a national government such as I propose will not put in conscription.
These are words for which hon. members have to take some responsibility. It was words of their leader that they all accepted. I am -taking some responsibility myself because I stated then and I state now that I was against conscription in the election of 1940, and no matter how much white-washing you try to do, the Conservative party and other parties without exception appealed to the Canadian voters on that basis in 1940.

speechtext: The Conservatives will still be muddled. '

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, I am no judge
of muddling. During that campaign-and I do not say it was done purely for political purposes, but during this time of crisis we
must start our discussions on an even keel- I remember that the late hon. member for Parkdale, Mr. David Spence, for whom everyone had such a high regard on account of his sincerity and integrity, when the Conservative party said they were going to burn their bridges behind them and run as a national government party, stated he was going to remain a Conservative, but they overruled him. They ran as a National Government .party and were defeated.
On February 24 last in this house the then Minister of Justice, the late lamented Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, asked the sitting members of the Conservative party whether they were adherents of the National Government party, and every one of them most definitely answered "No." At the present time they have a leader in the house, and I know his modesty will not be offended when I say he is a real Canadian and a real statesman. But if Mr. Meighen is elected in York South next Monday, what kind of following will he have? Because at the present time he is running as a National Government man, something that was absolutely repulsive to the Canadian electorate in the spring of 1940, and denied by the present sitting members.
I repeat that if we go at it in the proper way we could get by the voluntary system all the young men required for service overseas. In saying that, I am thinking not only of the whole of Canada but of my own constituency as well which has responded magnificently. We may have to put more glamour into the militia; we must improve our approach; but if proper methods are used, they can get the men that are needed. We know that at present great numbers of young Canadians want to get into the Royal Canadian Air Force. If it were possible for Canada and for the United States at the present time as well as Great Britain to send 10,000 young flyers with the proper equipment to Singapore, that great outpost of civilization and of British . power could be saved.
But I will go further-and I do not want to be misquoted; it seems it is always possible during a time of passion for certain newspapers to misquote everyone. During a recruiting campaign in my own constituency last fall I made it a point in speaking with the officers of that recruiting convoy to tell them that the onus and the responsibility rested primarily on their shoulders; that so far I was satisfied that the response had been not only spontaneous but unanimous and very loyal, but that the day might come when more sacrifice would have to be made and that if many did not answer the call of

The Address-Mr. Bradette
national need for the defence of civilization and Christianity, then the question would be left for themselves to answer; there could be no avoiding of responsibilities.
I want to say a few words about the new leader of the Conservative party. I believe I can do no better than give the charter that has been given to him by his own party by quoting from an article in Saturday Night of November 22, 1941, by the well-known editor of that paper, Mr. B. K. Sandwell, who is well posted on our Canadian life and affairs. This is what he has to say about the new leadership:
The terms of Mr. Meighen's acceptance of the Conservative leadership have revealed in a very clear light the nature of the strategy upon which the authors of the Meighen movement are relying, and which goes considerably further than was at first apparent. It is essentially a repetition of the strategy of 1917, and its design is to split off a sufficient fraction of the normal Liberal strength (first among the leaders of the party and members sitting in parliament, and then among the rank-and-file voters), partly by considerations relating to the vigour of the war effort, and partly by considerations relating to the country's railway problem, to ensure a popular vote against that party as soon as an election can be forced.
Those people who are against the plebiscite know well that their leader at the present time would be in favour of splitting this parliament to have a general election. Would they tell me that a general election would cost less than the plebiscite? I want them to be fair when they discuss such an important question, and tell the whole story.
This article continues:
The possibility of such an achievement, negligible in times of peace, becomes considerably greater in time of war when the dependence of the party on its solid Quebec support compels it to courses which many of its Englishspeaking members find it difficult to tolerate.
And again, further definition of that new charter of the great Conservative party:
One of these was the long-standing disagreement between the Liberals and Sir Clifford Sifton, which dated back to the establishment of separate schools in the newly constituted prairie provinces. But the overwhelming advantage which practically guaranteed the ability of the conscriptionists to win the election, and therefore made it easy for the dissident Liberals to come over to their camp, was the fact that they were already in control of the government and could manipulate the franchise as they wished. The War Times Election Act, of which Mr. Meighen was the author, conferred the franchise upon women relatives of members of the armed forces-
That was fine; that was the only redeeming feature of the whole thing, the only act that was not almost a criminal act.
-withdrew it from a considerable number of naturalized aliens, and authorized the chief returning officer-

I want parliament and this country to note this; I want those who were not old enough to vote in 1917 to listen to this:
-and authorized the chief returning officer to distribute the soldiers' vote among the constituencies at his own discretion. With these instruments at the government's disposal the result, even with a solid Quebec against it, was not in great doubt.
And they expect the Canadian people will fall for that again, as they fell for it in 1917. Once is enough. Some returned men told me personally that when they were in England fhey did not know their votes were going to be pooled; they did not know a reservoir was to be created, to be distributed at the whim of the chief returning officer, in any way that would suit the orders which he would receive. In my section of the country we do not want a repetition of that horrible thing, which occurred in the infamous election of 1917. During that election the fine farmers and citizens of the parishes of Moonbeam and Fauquier were entirely deprived of the right to vote. These parishes were fully nine miles apart, but had no road connection except the Canadian National right of way. The voters in Fauquier were told that they had to go to Moonbeam to vote; those in Moonbeam were told they had to go to Fauquier, and most of them spent all day walking back and forth, without being allowed to vote. In Porquis Junction there were twelve Liberal votes cast. Men wearing the uniform of the constabulary took those twelve votes and tore them up, so they were never counted. And they called that democracy. While the *country was fighting to destroy the principles of autocracy, we were suffering from the worst kind of autocracy this country ever experienced; trying to destroy the principle of free, universal suffrage; and as far as I am concerned, it will never be repeated. A good friend of mine, Eddie Lapierre, was elected in my constituency-it was my constituency at that time, taking in the two Cochranes and Nipissing-by over 1,200, by his own duly qualified electors. But after votes had been taken from that reservoir of soldier votes, he found himself defeated by forty. These are things we must remember at this time. I know no Conservative sitting in this House of Commons would be a party to any such unjust, unfair practices during the present crisis; however, this is the charter, drawn up by a man who is supposed to know, and appearing in a national newspaper read in every section of this country.
I should now like to say a word about the total-war committee. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) who said this afternoon that

The Address-Mr. Bradette
among the two hundred people present at that meeting were some fine gentlemen and fine ladies. But I could also tell the hon. member that many of those people went to that meeting without knowing why they had been called. In some cases-and1 this was told to me personally

they thought they were going to a meeting to promote the next war loan. Many of them did not even vote on the question; they remained in their seats, because they did not want to have anything to do with it. To me it smacks very much of Canada's wonder boy, who started that idiotic leadership movement which was stillborn a few years ago, the. young man who ' was going to run roughshod over every parliamentarian, making us all appear to be crooks and so on, and who eventually would become prime minister of this country. I have no fear of that last eventuality ever coming to pass.
I have tabulated each of these full-page total-war committee advertisements that I received from my constituents; and instead of these fine men and women of that committee spending large sums of money in a foolish effort to poison the minds of our electors in this province of Ontario, I think they should have found it possible to insert full-page advertisements in all the newspapers of Ontario in an endeavour to put over the new war loan, which is to be issued during the course of this month. In doing so, they would have been following some wonderful examples. For instance, I have in my hand a full-page advertisement appearing in that fine magazine Canadian Business, entitled "I Am Resolved." Resolved to do what?
I am resolved to be cheerful and uncomplaining at all times, sympathetic to those who work beside me, and to those in authority over me.
That is a much better principle than any enunciated by the total-war committee. Not long ago some ladies of the town of Timmins called me up and said they wanted to see me. I asked what it was about, and they said they wanted to start a total-war committee. I said, "I do not want one. I am converted to that principle and have been converted to it ever since the war started. Every citizen of this country is in favour of it." Then I added, "You must have some other work you can do, and that is helping the new war loan." Then this advertisement goes on to tell the Canadian people some other things they may do:
I am resolved to be tolerant of the shortcomings of others, realizing that to make an effort is commendable, to attempt nothing is deadly.
I am resolved gladly to do without some of those things I am accustomed to enjoy, for it
is good to deny oneself-even to suffer in a noble cause.
I am resolved that if I am fitted to serve my country best in the fighting forces, I will take my place proudly beside my comrades.
I am resolved to strive with all my power, to press on in my daily task to the limit of my endurance. It may be that my modest effort will tip the scale, and set a great shout of deliverance echoing 'round the world.
In this January number appear similar advertisements sponsored by the Northern Electric Company', Limited; Canadian Industries, Limited; British American Bank Note Company, Limited; Howard Smith Paper Mills Limited; Rapid Grip and Batten, Limited, and others; and on several occasions I have also received some wonderfully elevating, loyal Canadian and British literature from The Universal Life Assurance and Annuity Company of Winnipeg. I take this opportunity of thanking these people, and many others, that slip my mind at the moment, for their constructive work. I know that at least some of them are not political supporters of the present government, but they realize the duty of the moment.
We have a fine newspaper service in my constituency. We receive the Toronto morning papers as soon as they are available in Toronto itself; we know more about Toronto than they know about our section of the country. More than that, in my constituency I have one daily paper, one bi-weekly paper, and two weekly papers. In all these newspapers these full-page advertisements by the total-rvar committee appeared; and all told, I received forty-three letters as a result. This was' in a constituency with a population of over eighty thousand, and these letters would represent about 170 people. I acknowledged each of these letters, thanking the writer for the interest he was taking in our national affairs, in most instances making no comment. Neither did I make any comment when a mining engineer by the name of Stevenson took it upon himself to send an open telegram abusing the Prime Minister of this countiy. I do not intend to reply to that sort of abuse, because it is un-Canadian, it is unpatriotic. In our section of the country one man, whether he is a mucker working in the entrails of the earth, a farmer or a lumberman, is just as loyal as the next man. We know that this government is not perfect; but we also know that no matter what government is in power, we shall give it the same loyal support we gave the government of this country during the first great war.
I said the letters I received in response to these adv-ertisments represented a total of
The Address-Mr. Bradette

about 170 people. Hon. members will not be surprised, I hope, to learn that without propaganda of any sort I received communications from more than three hundred people during that period of time, telling me they were absolutely against conscription; because the only thing they could draw from that advertisement was that the answer to all our problems in connection with the war lay in manpower only. It is an important one, but there are also others. To me that is one very important subject, but there are other very important subjects as well. Canadians have cheerfully accepted many curtailments, and if they should be called upon to make further sacrifices, I know they will cheerfully do so. So far, casualties have been relatively low, but I resent the statement made both in parliament and outside parliament that in order for some to realize that we are in a war, we should have some bombing from the air. Perhaps for some people that might have a salutary effect; but no one who has seen or read or heard of what has happened in Europe, more particularly in valorous old England, is without fear in his heart and his eyes. We know what is going on. I say in the name of my own people that no matter what the. government may ask of us, be it bacon rationing, sugar rationing or egg rationing, we shall be willing to. cooperate.

speechtext:
I said that we are willing to do whatever we are asked to do. I do not want to be misquoted. I do not want the spirit of misrepresentation trying to speak here to-night. I am speaking with all sincerity. I never interrupt the hon. member when he is speaking, and I think I should have the same treatment from him. Last fall I listened to a broadcast by Mr. Donald Gordon of the priceceiling board. I do not have the pleasure of knowing that gentleman, but anyone listening to him would never doubt his sincerity. I should like to quote the last two paragraphs of the broadcast he gave when the price-ceiling policy was started. They are:
All of these probable hardships and mistakes and difficulties I fully realize and freely admit. I wish you to realize them too, because ten days from now, on Monday the 1st of December, you are going into a battle. You, wherever you may live, old or young, rich or poor, man or woman, are a soldier in this army. . . The board of which I am chairman is only the army headquarters. You are going to be the soldiers on the firing line and you must meet and conquer

doubts, fears, uncertainties, rumours, and alarms. You must keep always before you the one clear objective-prices must not rise; the price ceiling must be held; inflation must be beaten.
Forget the reasons why this policy will not work. Remember only that it must work, for there is no alternative except disaster.
This is your part in the war. In every home in Canada there is now a fighting part to play. I believe you can and will save yourselves and your- country in this crisis. I predict that the historian of a future day will record that when this call to duty came to you, you responded, not only with your loyalty but also with intelligence, imagination, and resource.
All Canadians should do whatever they possibly can to prevent inflation. We do not want inflation similar to what we had in 1917 and which brought ruin to every section of the country. If inflation should occur, then the help we are giving so generously and cheerfully to England will be absolutely meaningless, because our Canadian money will have practically no value whatever.
I should like to mention two or three matters with reference to my own section of the country. First of all I want to say that I am an upholder of the law; I believe in the principle of British and Canadian justice that when a man commits a crime, no matter who he may be, he should be brought before the courts. There are hundreds of thousands of young Canadians in training camps all over this country. Some of those from my section of the country are in camps located over a thousand miles from their homes. These boys sometimes go out on larks and do things not absolutely according to Hoyle. I hope it will be possible to have no' publicity given to these pranks. I want to be clear on this. If a criminal act is committed, such as manslaughter, highway robbery or anything of that kind, or wilful damage to property, then I want the law applied. However, many boys from the district of Cochrane are in camps at Ottawa, Camp Borden, Toronto and so on, and they sometimes get into a little trouble. The first thing we know this is spread all over the press in our section of the country. This is not the right kind of publicity to give to these boys. It is bad, not only for these young men but for their fathers and mothers living at home. They worry about this situation. Perhaps it would be possible to have these cases tried by a military court, at least they should be dealt with the same as military discipline is dealt with, and no publicity given to them.
I have one request to make. Like all members of parliament, I have always followed explicitly the lead that was given to us in the fall of 1939, that no political influence would

The Address-Mr. Bradette
have any bearing upon military matters. I believe, however, it is my duty to mention some anomalies that exist. The divisional registrar for our section of the country is a Mr. R. A. Irwin, located in Toronto. I am told, and I believe that this gentleman is most competent, but the fact that he resides in Toronto makes it necessary for young men in my section of the country who want to lodge appeals to go a distance of 880 miles. These young men want to do their duty, but there are instances where it is felt that an extension of time should be given. Because of the distance they must travel, many of these men do not get the extension and through correspondence the real situation cannot be known. I maintain that our rural, mining, industrial and pioneering population should have the same right of being heard before a divisional registrar as people living in any other section of the country. Again I want to say that I have nothing against this registrar, but I believe that some injustice is being done to those living in my section of the country.
During the debate I have listened attentively to such hon. members as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and other hon. members who live on the Atlantic coast. . I realize that all these hon. members were most sincere in what they said about the defence of the coasts of Canada. My section of the country is nationally and geographically the centre of Canada. Hudson bay and James bay cut this country almost in twain. I do not believe I am divulging any secret when I say that there are some defence works in the Bering strait. I am not going to state here what I stated a few months ago when some officers

these were not Canadian or British but allied officers-came to my section of the country and said that conditions there were not suitable for an air training school. I think that such judgments should be given by members of our own administration. Such a school should be possible in our section.
I should like to say a few words about criticism. We all maintain, and no doubt quite rightly, that criticism is absolutely necessary in a democracy under our parliamentary system. I believe it is, as long as it is constructive and not destructive. Certain sections of. the press, however, seem to be deliberately trying to poison the minds of our Canadian people in connection with our war effort. They are not at all fair to our government. I should like to quote briefly what Mr. Churchill said during a discussion last July. I quote:
I should like to give some facts and figures to show how the improved organization and the smoother running of our machines has overcome adverse currents.
This is rather easy money for critics who can oil a two-day debate with disparaging charges against our war effort.
Over-ardent or disaffected sections of the press can take it up and the whole give cry to a dismal cacophonous chorus of stinking fish all around the world.
Those are the things we have to fight against. I have in my hand what in my opinion is one of the most vicious, unfair and dastardly articles ever written by a newspaper.
I am referring to the Toronto Globe and Mail of January 31, 1942. The heading of the article is, "A disgrace to parliament." This article has reference to a speech delivered by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), and I believe he will highly resent this sort of editorial against our parliamentary system. I quote:
Shortly after he began his address, however, Prime Minister King motioned to his leading Quebec lieutenant-
Was there ever anything so sinister? Trying to intimate that the Prime Minister motioned deliberately to his leader from the province of Quebec to do an unfair act to my hon. friend. The article continues:
-and they showed their contempt for parliamentary procedure by walking out.
At the present moment there are only about half a dozen young men in the press gallery, but I would be the last one among the members of parliament here present to think for one moment that those who are absent are not carrying on their duties in their offices. No one will think of any other motive. It has never come to the mind of any member of parliament to doubt for one moment that the members of the press gallery, as well as the members of parliament, have duties to perform both inside and outside parliament. I continue:
Half the Liberal members present took the cue and followed. Among those remaining the small fry-
We are thankful for that expression.
-got so busy with conversation and heckling. . . .
I took the trouble to look up the record of the speech made by the hon. member for Parkdale, and I found that there was not one single bit of heckling from this side or any other part of the house.
The Address-Mr. Bmdette

There were several questions asked by the ministers, and I know the hon. member for Parkdale gladly answered them. The report in the Globe and Mail goes on to say:
Among those remaining the small fry got so busy with conversation and heckling that the Speaker had to call for order more than once. It is plain that what bothers these worshippers of party first is that Colonel Bruce has been so constructive in his suggestions that he has called the turn repeatedly and accurately on indifference and neglect.
We all agree with that. It goes on:
Not one of those who abused him has anything comparable to show for the time spent keeping the benches of the house warm. It would be difficult for them to indicate that they have done more than serve as rubber stamps.
The article winds up by saying:
This does not detract from the high character of the speech, a quality members of parliament must have learned to look for when the Toronto-Parkdale member gets on his feet. So they walk out lest they hear it, or heckle him in the hope he may falter. It is about as cheap a display of petty politics as could be found in the worst governed country.
If ever democracy is in danger, it is from attacks by that kind of article, the unfairness of which seeks to undermine and poison the mentality. I have been in this house for several years; I have always greatly enjoyed my associations with all the parliamentarians, and I know that I am voicing the sentiments of every member listening to me when I say that it would not occur to any of them to think a member was not true to his duty because upon some occasion he was not present in the house. A member is often called upon to leave the chamber to do something for his country or his constituency, something strictly pertaining to his own office, to attend to committee and departmental work, and that applies with all the greater force to the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet.
I took it upon myself, following this report, to find out what had actually occurred, and the Prime Minister will forgive me for mentioning that when he left the chamber he had an interview with the Governor General, Lord Athlone. I can assure the Globe and Mail that there was no sinister motive in the actions of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), a great Canadian and a fine parliamentarian. Hon. gentlemen opposite are frequently telling us to be easy on Toronto.
I know a lot of Toronto people, and ninety-nine and one-half per cent of them are fine, but this kind of journalism from Toronto is a shame to that city and to the rest of Canada.

There is another matter I want to mention, but I do not want to trespass on the time of the house.
