speechtext:
To sum up my conclusions, Mr. Speaker, this conflict has now been raging for. nearly two years and a half. It has developed into the most gigantic war conflagration that the world has ever witnessed, and nearly all the nations are embraced in its deadly grip.
I ask myself if at the present time we are not witnessing in our national and individual lives, some signs of lassitude, jagged nerves and destructive impatience. We must absolutely shake ourselves out of those unhealthy reactions, because a lot of effort and energy wasted on biased and destructive criticism could be much better employed in helping in the accentuation of our war activities and the surmounting of the problems emanating from them.
At a critical time like this no one should question the motives and sincerity of his fellow-Canadians. Let us put, in all our actions, the best that there is in us, so that the things we cherish so much will be safeguarded.	.
We have differences, we shall likely always have some, and the right to express and discuss them is one of the main pillars of democracy, but surely if we realize the fullness of our duty, we shall never cultivate in our minds the destructive virus of questioning our neighbours' loyalty and profound attachment and love for Canada and the British empire.
To come victorious out of this conflict ail the lovers of democracy will be required to unify their forces, and then, when the hour of victory strikes, we shall have a strong and unified nation that will be in a position to face the problems of our country and also of the post-war world.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much interest to the speech which has been made by the hon, member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). He has told us that he favours the plebiscite which his government proposes to take, but he has not told us during the course of his long speech whether or not, if the pflebiscite is taken and the government is relieved from the promises or pledges which it formerly made, he is in favour of national selective service. He has not told us whether or not he is in favour of the conscription of our

The Address-Mr. Hazen
man-power for service overseas in support of our forces over there. If I were to ask him that question to-night he might find it a little embarrassing. Perhaps he would not care to tell us this evening whether or not he favours national compulsory selective service in this country to-day.
I have observed, Mr. Speaker, since I entered this house that it is the usual custom of members who take part in the debate on the speech from the throne to congratulate first the mover and the seconder of the address upon the excellent speeches they made.
I do hot wish to appear unappreciative or impolite, but it is my intention this evening to depart from that practice and in the first place to extend my congratulations and sincere thanks to the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray) for the speech he made in this house last Tuesday afternoon..
Not only was that speech well constructed and well delivered, but it exhibited a courage, an intellectual honesty, a freedom from partisanship and a clearness of understanding that have not since I have been a member been equalled by any other speech to which I have listened.
No doubt that speech was not well received in all quarters, but I believe, sir, that it was acclaimed by the country, and if the hon. member for Lambton West received black looks from some he can find consolation if he needs it, although I doubt if he needs it, from part of a speech which was made on the same day in the British House of Commons by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, who said:
I have frequently -voted against governments which I have been elected to support, and looking back on it I sometimes felt very glad I did. Everyone in these rough times must do what he considers his duty.
It requires courage, Mr. Speaker, and visceral valour to place duty ahead of party but the hon. member for Lambton West has shown us that he possesses both these manly qualities.
A gentleman who once occupied a very prominent place in the press gallery of this house, not a very long time ago wrote a book in which he expressed the opinion that Canadian politicians, with few exceptions, put party politics first and other considerations nowhere. The hon. member for Lambton West has proved that he is one of the few exceptions.
I concur in almost everything he said. I wish I could have said it as well.
This plebiscite means delay; it means heartburning; it means bitterness.
It means also unjustifiable expense.
And when it is all over and the government is released from its pledge, the issue, as he says, still must be faced; and the bogy of national unity will again rear its ugly head.
In fact it has already commenced to do so.
I was particularly impressed with that portion of his speech in which he said:
Much has been and will be said of broken pledges. . . .
Does the hon. member forget that in the mother of all parliaments, Westminster, on April 27, 1939, while the nation was still at peace, and only four weeks after the then Prime Minister, Mr. Chamberlain, had renewed a pledge made by his predecessor, Mr. Baldwin, that compulsory military service would not be adopted, Mr. Chamberlain introduced a motion in these words:
"This house approves the proposal of his majesty's government to introduce as soon as possible a system of compulsory military training as announced on the 26th of April."
In the debate which followed the introduction of that motion, the prevailing opinion -was the same as it should be here in Canada: The facts are there and we must face them as they exist to-day. Let me suggest to the Prime Minister that whatever his declaration may have been, as our first minister in this hour of peril he is bound to act in accordance with what he believes is required for the national safety. That is the supreme pledge which he made, though perhaps not in words, when he assumed the high office which he now holds. What of the solemn pledge given by President Roosevelt during his last election campaign, to the effect that the forces of the United States would not be sent overseas? Within one month of the declaration of war we find the president telling congress^and the nation:
"We cannot wage this war in a defensive spirit. As our power and our resources are fully mobilized, we shall carry the attack against the enemy. American land, air and sea forces will take stations in the British isles-" Has there been any outcry in the United States of America against broken pledges?
I might tell the hon. member for Lambton West that I have heard no such outcries, but I have heard in this country a great outcry against the taking of this proposed plebiscite. I have received from my own constituents a number of communications protesting against it. I do not propose to read them into the record to-night, but one of them comes from the surviving members of the 26th battalion, a New Brunswick unit that had a distinguished record in the last war. It expresses strong disapproval of the plan, and states that the expense and time taken are unjustified and the spending of money for this purpose will 'have a decidedly adverse affect on the forthcoming war loan. With that opinion I am in hearty accord.
When I entered this house, Mr. Speaker, for the first time, a little over two years ago now, I
The Address-Mr. Hazen

ventured to express the opinion that it was no oeeasion for us to indulge either in platitudes or recriminations about past achievements or past failures of -the government, nor was it a time for us to play party politics, but it was our duty as Canadians to unite and, in our own interests, to do everything that lay in our power to bring this war, in which we had entered as a free nation, and in which our allies had suffered great reverses, to a victorious conclusion.
As time passed, I found no reason to change that opinion. As time passed I became more firmly convinced that party politics should be set aside if we were to make an effective allout war effort, and that this -war should not be carried on under any form of party government, but that it should be carried on under some form of union government which would have the support of all the parties in this house and would be free from petty partisan criticism, which has an adverse effect on our war effort.
As time passed, Mr. Speaker, the German army overran Denmark, Holland, Belgium and France. The British army, after sustaining heavy casualties, was forced to leave Dunkirk without arms or equipment. Italy declared war. France collapsed. The battle of the Atlantic was joined. Japan became a member of the axis. Italy invaded and Germany conquered heroic Greece. The allies were forced to withdraw from Crete. Germany, Italy and Roumania declared -war on Russia.
This is a very brief outline of the cavalcade of events which had presented themselves to members of this house before parliament reassembled in November last. It was not a reassuring picture. The situation that we faced as one of a group of nations fighting for our existence and the freedom of mankind afforded no ground for placid satisfaction. The situation demanded strong and courageous leadership. It demanded united action if an all-out effective effort was to be made.
On Wednesday, the fifth day of November last, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) made a report to this house on the work of his department. He had recently returned from England and had not had time to prepare a written address, but he made an excellent statement, and it was apparent to those who listened to him that he was a serious and determined man-two qualities which a minister of national defence should possess in war time. He told us-and to me this was the most important part of his address-that in the previous four months
37,000	men had been required for our army overseas and only 24,000 had been obtained. This meant that there was a shortage of about

thirty-five per cent in the numbers required to support our army overseas, and that at a time when there were no battle casualties.
Since then-if I may divert for a moment- our army has suffered heavy casualties at Hong Kong. But the courageous battle put up there by the Royal Rifles and the Winnipeg Grenadier Guards will rank, I believe, with the heroic defence made by the Rifle Brigade at Calais prior to the evacuation of Dunkirk. It was not a defeat, but it was a contribution to ultimate victory. The government was asked to send that force overseas on the 19th day of September last. It decided to do so ten days later, and I want here to-night to congratulate the Minister of National Defence and the government on the fact that they so promptly sent that force overseas when asked to do so by the army command.
A special committee of this house is to be set up at the request of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) to inquire into the reasons why untrained men were sent with that force, why those battalions lacked universal carriers, why their mechanical equipment, which means so much in this war, did not reach them in time. This should be done without delay, and if the committee find that there was negligence, complacency, military inefficiency, or lack of proper organization, appropriate action should be taken. But, sir, plans seldom work out perfectly in war time, and the work of this committee can in no way detract from the fact that the government sent that force when it was asked to do so; nor can it becloud the glory of these brave men who unflinchingly went forth and courageously did their duty. The people of this country and the members of this parliament must be firmly resolved that the sacrifice which those men made was not made in vain, and that we shall go on at all costs and all sacrifice until the evil thing which they fought against is destroyed. We cannot let our army that is overseas down. We must keep faith with those who die on foreign fields.
But to return to the report made by the Minister of National Defence on November 5 last; it was apparent from his report that the voluntary system of enlistment for overseas had fallen down, that it was not furnishing the men required. It was apparent that the situation should be reviewed and that a new policy should be adopted if we were to play our part as a nation of free men and women, if we were to hold our heads high in the world and meet total war with a total effort.
I realize that a new policy could not be brought about without courageous leadership, for it meant the breaking down of some

The Address-Mr. Hazen
political friendships and some old political ties. It meant also that certain old political ideas would have to be abandoned.
While we sat here in November I lived in the hope that something would be done. I hoped that the majority of the members of parliament, irrespective of party and of politics, could get together, forget party prejudices, and solve the problem of man-power for our army overseas.
Whatever hopes I had were dashed to the ground on the afternoon of November 12 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), late in the afternoon, came into the house-there were not many present at the time-and said that the people had decided against conscription at the last election and that, so far as he was concerned, without any consultation with the people on the subject, he did not intend to take the responsibility of supporting *any policy of conscription for service overseas.
That statement put an end to any hopes I had that action would be taken when action was needed.
I felt after that statement that I, as a Canadian, could no longer walk with pride among the nations of the world who were fighting for the freedom of mankind.
On my way home after the house adjourned on November 14, I had two experiences that did not raise my spirits. I met in Montreal an officer from the city in which I live, who was stationed at camp Petawawa. He told me that a short time previously a call had come to that camp for a draft of men for overseas service. The officer commanding the camp had about 600 men paraded. He told them of the order; he explained to them the situation; he asked for volunteers, and just nine men volunteered-nine of those men who were in uniform.
The same day in Montreal I met a young man, a connection of mine by marriage. His father was an Englishman, and his mother an American. When war broke out he was sixteen, living in England, and he came with his mother and sister to New York. When he was eighteen he came to Canada to enlist. He was turned down by the air force, enlisted in the army, was stationed at a camp near Montreal, and he expected to go overseas soon. He told me that soon after he arrived at that camp a draft for overseas had marched off. Eighty men had been called for to compose that draft, but eighty men did not leave that camp. If I remember his figures correctly-I did not write them down, but I think T have them approxi-[DOT] mately-that draft consisted of two Englishspeaking Canadians, twenty French-speaking Canadians, and thirty Americans. He told me the hut he was in held sixty-four men, and thirty of them were Americans.
Those Americans had joined the Canadian army when their own country was not at war, with the intention of going overseas to take part in the battle of freedom.
What could they have thought of those Canadians in uniform who held back after Canada had declared war and was fighting for her very existence?
And what would they have thought of those Canadian students in Montreal, who the other night, at Premier Godbout's meeting, opposed compulsory selective service, and kept qrying, "Canada, Canada only"?
There has been something very wrong in this country in the last twenty or twenty-five years. There has been lack of leadership of the right kind. There has been lack of clear thinking. There has been too much appeasement. There has been too much of the north American complex in some quarters.
But this is no time to rehash these matters. As I have said, I do not think we should indulge in recriminations about the past. I will put on the record no quotations from public men which are better left unsaid at the present time. This is a time when it is our duty to get on with the war and make an all-out war effort.
We adjourned here, as I said, on November 14 last. We reassembled on January 21, not very long ago. But modern war moves fast, and during that period while we were at home Japan treacherously attacked the United States and seriously damaged its navy; Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. Japan invaded Malay, attacked the Philippines, sank two of our capital ships, invaded Borneo, captured Penang, Wake island, Hong Kong, the Celebes, Tarakan, invaded Burma, the Bismarck archipelago and other islands and threatened Australia. The war in the east was going badly, and it is still going badly.
When we came back here we were told in the speech from the throne that this was the time of greatest crisis in the world's history. We were told also that unless the enemy were defeated, the free people of the world, one after the other, would be reduced to a state of bondage.
I find no fault with those statements; I agree with them.
But what did the government propose doing in view of the situation?

The Address-Mr. Hazen
It proposed to take a plebiscite! It proposed to ask the people of this country, after a certain amount of time has passed, a question to this effect:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
Does the Prime Minister of this country take that course because of a pledge he has given? Does he take it because he has to be scrupulously consistent in all things? It has been pointed out during this debate that English and American statesmen did not let consistency stop them from taking immediate action when the safety of the state was in danger. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that he ponder the words of one of America's greatest teachers and writers; it was Ralph Waldo Emerson who said that a foolish consistency was the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen, philosophers and divines. And I might say that I once read somewhere that the only completely consistent people are the dead.
The Prime Minister in the statement he made on November 12 last said:
I do not intend to take the responsibility-
There have been other occasions in the past in which he got out of taking responsibility by referring his difficulties to a royal commission or a judicial tribunal. He cannot do that on this occasion, so he proposes to take a plebiscite. I protest against it. I consider it unwise; I consider it dangerous.
I appeal to hon. members, irrespective of party, and particularly to those who served in the last war, and who are willing to serve again, to the members who are in uniform, to the men who have sons overseas and relatives overseas; to the men who want to make an all-out war effort. I appeal to them and ask them if there is no way that we can go to the Prime Minister and ask him to abandon this plebiscite that he proposes taking.
There are a number of reasons why this idea of a plebiscite should be abandoned. The most important one I think is that if it proceeds we run a very grave danger. That danger is this, that it is quite possible it will seriously injure the object that all of us, or almost all of us, have in mind and want to achieve; that is to have Canada make an all-out effective war effort, and1 support our army overseas. That danger should be avoided. The government should take a firm grip of the situation, tell the people what they have to do and then see that they do it. All that loyal Canadians are asking for in this crisis is leadership.
*Mr. Hazen. 1

speechtext:
As a, member from the city of Winnipeg I think it both natural and appropriate that my first words in this chamber during this session should be a tribute to those fellow townsmen of mine who fought the Canadian fight in the city of Hong Kong. I wish publicly to pay my respects to them and to offer my sympathy to those who wait with anxious hearts to know the fate of those whom we sent there.
I should like to say to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Power) that I believe anybody in Canada faced with the decision that he had to make would have agreed to send two battalions to Hong Kong and I am quite sure that that decision was a matter of complete agreement on the part of the government and would have been completely agreed to by any hon. member.
While I am on the subject of those men in Hong Kong, I should like to say further that I think it is contemptible that the agony of heart and mind which the loved ones of those men who went to Hong Kong are suffering should have been aggravated to help in a by-election, by what I consider unwarranted assumptions about the inefficiency of at least one of those battalions. However, the matter is being investigated, or will be, and I hope that when the investigation comes, it will not be trial by newspaper as has been the situation in some instances in Canadian political history. I hope that if anyone was culpable in the preparation for sending those men to that far-off battle field, the culpability will be made apparent and suitable punishment meted out, not in a spirit of revenge, but in order that that type of thing, if it happened, shall not happen again to the thousands who will follow them to the battlefields of this war.
I wanted to begin that way rather than in the conventional way of addressing congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, because naturally that expedition and the fate of those men are uppermost in my mind. But I should like to say to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply that I have at least paid them the, for me, unusual compliment of having read their speeches, as I was not in the chamber to hear them.
It is, however, not of the glory of the dead, or of the accomplishments of the living that I wish to speak for a few minutes to-night, but rather of the Canadian soldiers, and not so much of what we can rightly expect from them, but of what they in my opinion have a right to expect from us. I have a special contempt for the cheap, shoddy device of the demagogue, the tvpe of parish-pump politics

The Address-Mr. Mutch
by means of which any man in parliament, or in a newspaper, or anywhere else attempts to further his own ambitions or those of his party, or to give expression to his own malice, in the name of service men.
I have some recollections of the last war. As a youngster of nineteen or twenty I remember those all too infrequent occasions when we got hold of newspapers from Canada and read some of the profound remarks of the barber-shop strategists; I remember something of what we thought and felt. I am sorry to say that not only in some newspapers, but also in places where they should know better, we still encounter some of that same kind of platitudinous tripe. I think I speak for all the nearly a quarter of a million, perhaps more-we do not give figures -of Canadian-born soldiers who are on active service in this war when I say they share the feeling of distaste which I experience when I consider the antics of certain people in Canada who I think are best described as "Little Canadians." I refer to those belittlers of Canada and Canada's contribution to the war effort. People of this kind thrived and multiplied during the dirt and despair of the depression; and with the outbreak of war they multiplied again. They see only the efforts of someone far away and turn a jaundiced eye, if they look at all, toward the miracles of accomplishment that have taken place in their own country.
I am not one of those who think we need fear to boast a little about what we as Canadians have accomplished. If I have any fear at all, it is only that some of us, looking at those accomplishments, may fall into the equally dangerous and perhaps more natural folly of being too easily satisfied. Neither am I one of those who think the government did it all, even though I would include in that the whole House of Commons'. I realize, as I think it is realized by every thinking person in Canada and everyone outside Canada who knows of our effort, that what has been done could not have been accomplished without a high degree of cooperation between the ordinary man and woman on the street and the government. It would have been simply impossible; and when we brag a little, as I think we might, we should remember that. It is the work of all Canadians. And if, instead of making a cult of criticism, w'e would look about us once in a while and see how we can help our general effort, then magnificent as it has been, that effort might be made much greater yet.
If I might make a personal reference, Mr. Speaker, I have worn his majesty's uniform for nearly five years. I do not profess to be a soldier. I do not know that my personal
loyalty has been attacked, nor would I stoop to defend it if it were. What I have to say is of my own determination, the result of my own experience and thought. I begin by saying that in my considered opinion most of the organized-and I ask the house to note that word "organized"-effort for the adoption of the slogan "selective service" is pure humbug. I do not question the sincerity of thousands of persons who have been caught by the unanswerable, reasonableness of that slogan. To them it has become a sort of magic formula, and many of them have the thought that without that formula being brought into operation, Canada cannot measure up to that other slogan, "an all-out effort."
I do not pay very much attention to the clamour of some public men, or to the propaganda of a subsidized press. I am of opinion that much of the effort behind this slogan of selective service is either an insincere political effort or a sort of half-hearted sabotage, not of Canada's war effort but of those who are attempting to administer that war effort in these trying times. The promoters of the current political ramp-because we are all well aware that this is just what is in the process of organization to-day-are all much too well informed to believe that this catch-phrase can accomplish those things which are promised for it. They know as well as any member of this house knows, and better than most, that a big army policy for Canada, for instance, is pure lunacy; but they make an emotional appeal in order to cloak their real motive, which is to tear down a government which believes, and practises the belief, that a generation which makes war should pay for it.
There are thousands of men in this country who fought during some part of the last war and who came home to help pay for it. They have made a magnificent contribution in helping pay for it. Perhaps at times they have been a bit cynical about it, but during troublesome times in every part of the country they have been a sort of safe and sane centre, a. hard core of realism and reality. They have paid generously and generally willingly, but many of them have also determined that as far as is humanly possible they will go along with the policies of the present administration to the end that the legacy of debt and depression may be at least less than it was after the last war.
Then in times like these we hear a great deal about equality of sacrifice. I do not propose to say a great deal about that, but once or twice before in this house I have made the remark that the expression has no reality.
The Address-Mr. Mutch

War is not cricket or baseball; it is not a sporting event, or anything of that kind. War is the brutal business of destruction on the one hand and self-preservation on the other. The only possible sort of equality of sacrifice in a situation like this is when every man and woman in the country is voluntarily giving everything he or she has to give. And because that definition does not admit of realization is no reason why we as Canadians should not strive toward that goal. There is no reason why in our individual and governmental enterprise we should not do what we can to level the burden. War is not a question of taking what one can get with the least possible sacrifice. It is a question of taking what one needs wherever he can get it, and not paying for it unless he has to. That is the spirit of it; that is the ruthless basis of war. It is extermination or survival; and if that was perhaps only figuratively true in other wars, most of us should be convinced by now that it is literally true in this one.
I said that this ideal was perhaps not capable of realization, because the rich young man of biblical times who turned sadly away, has too many descendants in this modem, imperfect world. The poorest and most unhappy of his descendants are not blessed with worldly goods, as he was, but are poor. But, though poor in worldly goods, unfortunately their greatest poverty. is of the spirit; and any conception of an all-out sacrifice, about which we talk so glibly and of which the editorial writers and even some of our newsmen speak with such facility, is simply meaningless, because we have not reached the point where mankind is equal to it. If we are realists, selective service boils down to conscription for overseas service. I know that many earnest, well-meaning people will disagree with that statement. They will argue that selective service means taking the right man and putting him in the right place, eliminating all square pegs in round holes. We may not have another five or seven years of war to accomplish that, and in the meantime the war is catching up with us.
I should like to make one or two personal statements with respect to the policies enunciated in the speech from the throne and the methods undertaken by the government to cany them out. First I want to say that as a member of this house, as a soldier with some experience in the last war, as one who was born in this country of purely British descent, I am perhaps one of the most reluctant conscriptionists. Further, should I be convinced, or when I am convinced-I admit freely that I foresee the probability, or
tMr. Mutch.]
at least the possibility of that time coming

I would take the last son from the last widow in Canada and send him away if I were convinced that, by doing that, Canada would be making her greatest contribution to the winning of this war.
I do not believe that there are many people in this country who disagree with what I have just announced should be done in that circumstance. There is an honest difference of opinion as to the desirability of conscription now. I am prepared to give to those who believe that there is an all-out urgency for conscription for overseas service now- that is what I am talking about-the right to their opinion, but at the moment I stand unconvinced. If we vrere all agreed that we did not need conscription now, it might happen that within forty-eight hours we would be shown that we were wrong. If we have learned nothing else as a result of the progress of this war, we should have learned that there is no finality of decision with respect to how we should proceed. Only amateur historians or those who have been called barber shop tacticians have the effrontery to assume any finality for their plans in a conflict which is world-wide and ever shifting.
I should like to say to the members of the cabinet here to-night that the government should give us an inventory and a plan of our man-pow'er, and it should be given to us now. It must be elastic, but it could be given within reasonable limits. They must know our resources, and it is only when we know what our potential objectives are with respect to production, that we can measure the success or the failure of the methods which we are presently employing. As far as I am concerned, my only assets are a good name and the respect of my fellow men. In my election of 1940, either through what I said myself or what was said on my behalf, I believe that conscription was not a factor.
If I agreed, which I do not, that to-morrow, or within a matter of days or hours or short weeks, conscription was essential and that had been the decision of the government, speaking for myself my conscience would be perfectly clear in supporting the government in that decision. But, because my leader elects to trust those who have trusted him so often, I shall not help to throw him to the political jackals, if you like, who thirst for his political blood. I think I speak fairly when I say that my constituents would favour conscription to win the war, and I believe I am correct when I say that many of them favour it now.
Speaking in this place to which they have sent me, I have this to say to them: Make

The Address-Mr. Mutch
your support of the plebiscite overwhelming. In the hour when my judgment and conscience says that we must change any policy so far as I am concerned no sense of loyalty to person or party will deter me from what I conceive to be my duty. I say to them that such a majority as I have requested from them, and from all Canadians, will clear the way for any eventuality.
Because war is a function of government it does not necessarily follow that members of parliament are military strategists. One of the first and most important things which we who attempt to give some guidance to the new recruit coming into our army have to do is to teach him to think as a soldier. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the difference in thinking between the man who is a good citizen as a civilian and the man who is a good soldier is as wide as the poles. The measure of our success and of the usefulness of the recruit who comes into the service is very often the measure of the degree to which we succeed in teaching him to think as a soldier. I think some of us have forgotten that there is a difference between the thinking which goes with military effectiveness, with campaign effectiveness and that which goes with civilian effectiveness.
Some of these military strategists have spoken to us of sending a division to Australia.
I should like to address a few questions to those who hold that view. Have they ever determined how many ships it would take to transport one division of men and their equipment, to say nothing of how long that tonnage would be tied up in transit? I should like to ask them, where are the ships to take them, and where are the ships to convoy them? Then I would ask them: Have you discovered for yourselves where the equipment is? Then I think we might add one more question: Who has asked for the men?
Remember France, Greece, Crete, Libya, Hong Kong and now Singapore. I think in each and every case the reverses which our forces have suffered have been due not so much to lack of man-power as to lack of an aeroplane roof over their heads and lack of communications. I wonder how long Australia would be worried about a Japanese invasion by sea if she had at her disposal a really adequate air force. I wonder how many strait of Macassar battles the Japanese invading forces could stand up to if that was their daily dish. I wonder what Australian cities would be bombed, even from aircraft carriers of the Japanese fleet, if Australia had the formidable air support which she will need, and which, please God, she will have before this battle is over. I wonder when people with the best
intentions in the world will stop expecting the miracle of David and Goliath to be reenacted on every fresh front. I wonder when we are going to stop asking our brave and courageous soldiers to step into the breach with only their courage and rifles and small automatic arms and stem the mechanized might of our enemies who have a preponderance of attacking air force.
I doubt the wisdom of any considerable expansion in the Canadian overseas army. In this war of wide sweeps and deep objectives, with failures of communication and mechanical failures and casualties, such as we have seen in Hong Kong, one hundred per cent losses are not an impossibility. I wish I could think that they are not even a probability.
I urge that the government decide now whether our young men between the ages of nineteen and twenty-nine, which is the age when they are most- valuable, shall serve Canada in the armed forces of Canada or whether they can make a greater contribution to the war effort of our allies and ourselves in the air. I do not know the answer, but if the government has not determined it, I do urge that they determine it and then let us know what their policies are. Having decided in which branch our young men shall serve, we should then determine what strength of forces we can raise and equip; and having determined that, I would expend every ounce of Canadian energy to see that those men were given the chance that brave men deserve in the way of providing them with proper equipment and adequate reinforcements so that they can meet on equal terms men, no matter whether they be lesser men than we are, who, if they are better equipped than our forces, will present difficulties which will make our losses out of all proportion to what they should be. Some day somebody in this country will have to do a little simple arithmetic. Why not now? Let us know the objective with respect to our military development and what our maximum effort can be. That can easily be determined if one takes out of this question all the sentiment and emotional drivel with which it is wrapped up, and look instead at the vital statistics. Then tell us what the answer is in terms of war effort with respect to our army, air force, and navy, and with respect to our industrial effort and the production of food. These facts are not unobtainable. Just a little simple arithmetic would give us all a better idea of where we are going than we have now. When this is determined I am prepared to support a policy which will stop at nothing to see that these men have everything that is necessary to achieve our share of victory with
The Address-Mr. Mutch

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in March, 1940, six months after the declaration of war, the Canadian nation gave the Liberal party a majority unprecedented in our political history. On that occasion the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was elected on a platform whereby Canada, engaged of its own free will in war at the side of Great Britain, was to provide a voluntary and moderate cooperation commensurate with its resources and financial capacity. This platform also contained a pledge that no union government would ever be sought by a Liberal administration and that compulsory military service would never be enacted for overseas. This programme obtained the overwhelming support of the Canadian people.
For the past two years the Prime Minister has conducted the ship of state with a mastery which does honour to his great qualities as a parliamentarian and to the confidence placed in him. Together with the late Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe, whose passing is still deeply regretted, he has worked to keep the country united and to guard against the errors and abuses of the last war. Never has the Canadian nation been more united than during the past two years. Never has there been enacted legislation better fitted to paralyze the appetites of war profiteers and to protect the lower classes of society. The system of voluntary enlistment, endorsed by the electors, has given excellent results, since 400,000 Canadians are at present ready to serve voluntarily in any theatre of war anywhere in the world. In the face of the Hitler menace which was spreading even to the new world, the Prime Minister proposed in 1940 his National Resources Mobilization Act for the defence of Canada which was accepted if not with alacrity, at least with the patriotism which every citizen owes to his country in time of peril. When this act was brought down it produced certain reactions. But the Prime Minister is able to say now with pride that he gauged the situation correctly. If this act had not been passed at that time and if measures for the defence of the country had to be placed in hand now, what a problem would we not face to-day?
The Prime Minister asked of the people of Canada for sacrifices of all kinds in contributions and in taxation; the Canadian people accepted these sacrifices with pride and patriotism. Millions of dollars have been spent in direct aid to the allies. Canada has generously exceeded the collaboration she promised. Millions of dollars have been expended to levy and equip troops for service overseas. I greatly admire those volunteers who are serving abroad and I salute those who have died, less
for their own country than for the great cause of world freedom. Millions of dollars have been spent for the construction of immense munitions plants and for the organization of our own'defence in every domain. The free, voluntary and moderate effort promised in 1940 has certainly broadened out, but can the government be blamed for that? I voted as a free and honest man in favour of the mobilization for the defence of my country.
In refusing to form a union cabinet, the government respected a solemn promise. It would have been a sacrilege to allow the politicians of the list war, on whose policies the people have already passed judgment, to share in * the administration of the country without having received a mandate 'therefor.
I consider that the government have accomplished a great task for the allies, a task so great that I sometimes wonder if it has not jeopardized our national defence. However, we must to-day face the fact that we shall have, from now on, to look more carefully after our own defence. Canada has a vast area to defend and has by no means a large population to do it. We shall soon enter the fourth year of war, with the spectacle of a convulsed world. Whither are we going? No one can tell. We are told in the speech from the throne that this is a time of gravest crisis. I believe that. I also believe that Canada is threatened. It is possible and even probable that our countiy may soon feel the horrors of war. More than ever Canada must think of the defence of her own territory, and proceed at full speed with the work in hand. I for one am not prepared to support any measure or legislation which would not have that primary object in view.
Can I, then, accept the idea of a plebiscite, as expressed in the speech from the throne, and especially the question which is to be put before the electors? In all frankness I say no. Is the question as asked a clever move on the part of the government to dodge the attacks of persistent enemies and perhaps also to silence those who, even in the government itself, oppose the 1940 programme? The question looks so much like camouflage that, in spite of the deep respect I have for my party, I cannot accept it. There is perhaps no member of this house-I do not say it boastfully-who, during the last two years, has contributed more than I to the war effort of this country. I have given my active and unqualified support to all war organizations: loans, war savings certificates, Red Cross, Canadian war services fund, salvage campaign, and so forth. I have given my full moral support to the soldiers who have been trained in my constituency, and I have frequently visited
252	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
and encouraged them. During the last year, I have given all my attention to the creation and organization of extensive shops at Sainte-Therese. The Allied War Supplies Corporation and Defence Industries Ltd. c&n vouch for the unselfish cooperation I have given them. 'My paper has been used in the furtherance of the common cause, and everywhere in my constituency I have never ceased to advocate cooperation with the allies and the defence of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I am neither a nationalist nor a separatist. I love my province, and I am proud of it, but I consider myself above all a Canadian. I hate racial strife and prejudice, which in the past have only served to destroy the harmony necessary to the national development. That is why any movement based upon a narrow nationalism is contrary to my conception of true patriotism.
I admire Great Britain, which for the last two years has given the world a wonderful lesson of courage, steadfastness and patriotism. In her misfortune I sympathize with France, and I still admire her. I believe in her resurrection, because France, like England, can not die. That resurrection will come through the united effort of all the democracies. I do not begrudge the old world the ammunitions, the food, and the volunteers we have given it during the last two years; we have done all that because we wished to see democracy survive as the leading force in the world.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, 400,000 of our men may, through the terms of their enlistment, serve anywhere in the world. In two years only, we have spent many billions of dollars for war and our national debt is increasing at such a rate that we shall perhaps never be able to straighten it out again. What of it? I would rather see my country come out of this war impoverished but proud and free. That conscription in Canada for overseas service will change the world situation is something I do not believe. That conscription for overseas, at this critical stage of our history, can prove advantageous, I believe still less. To impose it would* be a crime. The defence of the country calls for our undivided attention. Being vulnerable on every side, has not the country first claim to our solicitude? Our country needs all its man-power for national defence, at home, on the farm and in the factories. Must we have to face invasion without sufficient military strength to defend our shores and our land? What has Australia done? The world over, to every battle front, for two years now, she has sent her best soldiers; to-day, lacking sufficient man-power to meet impending dan-
ger, a stern reality to-morrow, she calls out for help. What a mistake!
Conscriptionist Conservatives, indeed, have not departed from their wonted doctrine. The members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are almost fully in accord with them. They will not get my vote. Nor will the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). For this is 1917 all over again. For with these Conservatives, ten times more conservative than the ordinary Conservative, we find ourselves, just like in 1917, before the same setting, the same programme, the same zeal, the same enthusiasm. They hold the same prejudices and the same fanaticism. Indeed, we find. the same faces and the same interests. Had this party been in power, conscription for overseas service would have been on the statute books long since. What is unity to them? Why should they not approve voluntary service? Were it a good thing, still would they turn away from it and* endeavour to prevent it. Nevertheless, they are aware of the opposition existing against conscription for overseas service in every section of the country.
The only objective of their whirlwind campaign is conscription and power with a return of the shameless patronage of 1917. Instead of propaganda for overseas service, instead of millions to win over public opinion, why should not Mr. Meighen, Mr. Hanson and their friends devote the same zeal, the same enthusiasm, the thousands of dollars in publicity for voluntary service, to promote it and improve its results? Their bad faith stands out too clearly to require that it should be unmasked now. Conscription? Why, it *would set Canadian against Canadian in every province of this Dominion; it -would at one fell blow destroy national unity forged through years of concession, effort and mutual understanding; it does not add anything to the valour of our troops, for experience teaches that ten conscripted men are not worth one voluntary soldier. I intend voting, therefore, against the sub-amendment proposed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and against the amendment presented by the hon. leader of the opposition, because conscription for overseas is a measure both unpatriotic and contrary in every way to Canadian security.
Nor am I in favour of the question proposed for the plebiscite. A plebiscite is indeed a democratic form of consultation and the government shows, in taking such a course, a desire to know public opinion in the land. We are invited, however, to release the government of its commitments. This I cannot do, because I am satisfied with them. I am

The Address-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
requested to obtain, release from my own commitments; my constituents, whom I know well, are opposing this already. The government wishes to be released from its obligations. Why? Does not its term of office extend to three more years? Or should it abdicate to please certain dissident Liberals? Has it weakened under pressure from the imperialistic group from Toronto who, without mandate, wish to govern the nation? Do they wish to gain time? The government states they desire release from previous commitments in order to be free to adopt all necessary measures dictated by circumstances. I understand that it is not implied that the present administration will necessarily enact conscription if released from its commitments; however, there is always the danger and the possibility that it will be enacted.
What will be the result of the plebiscite? If the Canadian people answer "No", so much the better. If the answer should be "Yes", the imperialistic press campaign, imbued with prejudice, armed with threats and invectives, will be revived, stronger, more irreverent, more audacious than before. What then? The government, released from past commitments, may have to yield to renewed pressure both from within and without. This is giving the government a blank cheque together with the power of filling it at discretion. If this cheque were handed personally to the Prime Minister or the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) or some other minister, I state, for the benefit of my constituents, that I would be willing to take the chance. But, who could be sure that the war will be over in two or three years? Who will promise that Mr. King will still be with us in six months? Who will give assurance that Mr. Cardin will be there? Men may disappear suddenly and this truth has been brought home to us only recently. Those men gone, could I be positive that the new incumbent, armed with the blank cheque, would not be too willing, with the consent of a parliament become amenable, or a parliament transformed and favourable to him, to use it at will? I cannot risk such a contingency. I will possibly be accused of forsaking my party. Still I should have the satisfaction, which neither fame nor honours may replace, of having been faithful to my mandate and my conscience. I am a Liberal and a Liberal I shall remain, for, in my opinion, this party stands for freedom of speech. Moreover, I am convinced that my frankness will be useful to my party. I was elected in 1940, because I was supporting a certain political platform; the sincerity of those who elected me left no room for doubt. I am not going to organize a new party, nor
to join any new group whether under the name of "Canadian" or "National" party. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to support sub-amendments which, after all, would have the same effect as the main motion and are consequently useless-and above all, when they are moved by hon. members sitting on the other side of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I shall return to my constituency, but I am too well acquainted, with the opinions of the voters there to ask them to release the government from its past commitments. I am already too positive that they have enough faith in Mr. King to answer the plebiscite in the affirmative and that he is the man whom they wish to see in power. However, I shall say to my constituents: "consider first your country which you are bound to defend. Remember Australia. Do not repeat the same mistake. What you must defend is your homes and your rights, every inch of Canadian soil, from Vancouver to Halifax," and they will not fail to understand. I shall say to them: while some of our sons stand guard over our country, ready to make the supreme sacrifice, our soil must produce food for our armies and those of our allies; I shall say to them that farmers and their sons must stick to their ploughs and furrows and they will understand. I shall also tell them that our factories must have men to produce the tools of victory, and everyone, man, woman, girl and *boy will understand. I shall instruct the young men to rally to the defence of their country, worthy of the best we have to offer, even life itself. If you wish to try your luck, if you think that it is your diuty to go over there, overseas, if you want to go into action, do not hesitate, enlist voluntarily, and they will understand. All my people of the "highlands" whose courage has been sung by Valdombre know that the defence of one's country is a sacred obligation. They will not say that their country ends with the confines of the province of Quebec, but that along with their own province they hold dear all of their country from the granite boulders of the Rocky mountains to the sod of the plains of Nova Scotia.
I shall therefore vote against the address in reply to the speech from the throne and express the wish that the country's answer to the plebiscite be "No." I hope that from this negative answer will be born the sincere desire to serve our country better. I hope that the Prime Minister will continue to stand by the platform of 1940 which, to my mind, expressed the true aspirations of the Canadian nation. Let us collaborate with the allies but with all our will keep our man-power for the noble task of defending Canada first.
